objectives: Identify the source the introduction names and the claims it makes about Adam (pbuh), the story and Satan.
Explain the difference between “a rebel against Allah’s command” and “a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah”.
Discover how the introduction names its source, uses the passive to keep its topic in front, and corrects or narrows ideas (not … but …, rather than).
Explain why a “factual tale” can still be read for lessons and morals.
content.pedagogy: Start with the job of an introduction: Learners predict what a writer must do before telling a story (name a source, choose a focus, rule out a wrong reading). While reading, they label sentences with three colored symbols (source / focus / correction). Grammar is discovered from these labels: You ask “Who tells the story in ‘The story … is told …’? Why is that not at the front?” and learners work out the purpose of the passive before you confirm it.
priorKnowledge: Active and passive forms; basic contrast with but; the idea of a source.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reading Satan as a rival of Allah: The text says he is a rebel against Allah’s command but a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) “rather than Allah”.
“Fabulous” here means remarkable, not fable-like: The text says the tale is “not symbolic or imaginary”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: source-grounding (We learn his story from …, Based on …) · passive for topic focus (He was created from clay …, The story of Adam (pbuh) is told …, Satan is portrayed as …) · correcting and narrowing (not symbolic or imaginary, but … / a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah) · summarising without losing a distinction.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort seven parts of the text by job. Ask: “In ‘The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an’, who tells the story, and why is the story at the front?” and “What does ‘rather than Allah’ take away?”
Build (Activities 2–3): reframe the same claims (… an original factual tale rather than … / The Holy Qur’an tells … / These surahs portray …), then choose the summary that keeps both the rebellion and the narrowed rivalry.
Likely errors: *is portrayed like a rebel · *The story is tell · “rather than” read as “and” (enemy of both) · dropping the source from a summary.
Use (Activity 4): a 6–8 sentence source-aware paragraph about another account the learners know, with one source frame, one deliberate passive, one rather / rather than and one clear contrast.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the source frame and pause after it: “BASED on the HOly QurAN, | the creAtion of ADam …”.
Weak forms in passives: “was /wəz/ creAted”, “is TOLD”, “is PORtrayed as /əz/ a REBel”.
Contrastive stress: “NOT SYMbolic or iMAGinary, | but … FACtual”, “an ENemy of ADam | RAther than alLAH”.
Word focus: mi-RAC-u-lous, phil-o-SOPH-i-cal, his-TOR-i-cal, por-TRAYED, sym-BOL-ic.
beforeReading: Ask: “Before a writer tells an important story, what three things should the introduction do?” Pairs suggest ideas (say where it comes from, say what kind of story it is, rule out a wrong reading). Keep them on the board as predictions.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Which of our three predictions does the introduction do?
Mark the source phrases (We learn … from, Based on).
Underline the three passives and ask who the doer is in each.
Box the two corrections: “not symbolic or imaginary, but …” and “rather than Allah”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the source phrases in view.
Language Focus: Sort source / focus / correction in Activity 1, reframe in Activity 2 and choose the accurate summary in Activity 3.
Write a 6–8 sentence source-aware paragraph about another account (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What must an introduction do?” pairs give three predictions, you keep them on the board; 4–12 Listen with books closed (which prediction is confirmed?), then read along and mark source phrases and corrections; 12–18 Three-symbol labelling in pairs (S = source, F = focus/passive, C = correction), quick whole-class check of the Satan sentence: Rebel against a command / enemy of Adam; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Who tells the story? Why is the story first?), Activities 2–3 in pairs with a short check of “rather than”; 31–38 Use: Learners draft the Activity 4 paragraph about a history or literature text they know, partner circles the source frame and the passive; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer name the source in the first lines?
What would change if “rather than Allah” became “and Allah”?
How can a text be “an original factual tale” and still give “many lessons and morals”?
interactiveTips: Use The First Prophet hotspot after learners have found “the first human being to be created, and the first prophet”.
Use the Creation and Moral Choice hotspot with the last sentence about “a division and contrast between good and evil”.
Replay the Satan sentence and ask learners to count the two claims they hear.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give three labels with one example each and the frames “We learn … from ____.”, “____ is portrayed as ____.” and “It is ____ rather than ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite two claims from the introduction in the active voice and explain in one sentence why the writer preferred the passive.

formativeAssessment: Names the source correctly.
Keeps the rebel / enemy distinction in a summary.
Explains the purpose of one passive and one correction.
expectedResponses: The introduction names the Holy Qur’an as its source, presents the tale as factual rather than symbolic, and portrays Satan as a rebel against Allah’s command and as the enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than a rival of Allah.
content.transferTask: Write a short source-aware introduction to another account you know, naming its source and ruling out one wrong reading.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover why the passive keeps the topic in front before I named it, and did their summaries keep the “rather than” distinction?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, label the introduction with three symbols: S for a source, F for a passive that puts something in focus, C for a correction. Be ready to justify one label of each kind.
checkQuestions: What does C mark? (a correction or narrowing)
How many labels do you justify? (one of each kind)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen during the whole-class check for the Satan sentence: learners should keep “rebel against a command” and “enemy of Adam” apart. In the Use task, check that partners circle a real source frame and not just any past verb.

exitTicket: Write one sentence that names a source and one that corrects an idea with “rather than”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the Qur’an as the source and quotes the frame that shows it.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the first paragraph and ask “Where does the writer say the story comes from?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why one passive puts the focus on the thing done.
rubricLevels.notYet: Turn the passive into an active sentence and ask what moved to the front.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains how “rather than” corrects or narrows a view.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “The story is presented as … rather than …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a connected paragraph with a source frame and a passive.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three-sentence outline: source, focus, correction.

interculturalFocus.notice: The introduction names its source and narrows one reading ('a rival and enemy of Adam rather than Allah'). Naming sources is a writing convention valued in academic English.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: When Turkish school texts tell a historical or religious account, how do they show the source? How does an English encyclopedia or school book do it (According to …, footnotes, references)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners see that citing a source is not distrust of the story but respect for the reader. They write one source line in each convention.

objectives: Explain how the terms earth, water and clay relate to one material and its stages.
Trace the chain from verse and hadith evidence to the conclusion about shared origin and no superiority.
Discover the difference between a defining and a non-defining relative clause, and the linkers that move from example to conclusion to correction.
Separate human diversity from ranking, as the chapter does.
content.pedagogy: Build an explanation chain on the board: terms → definition → example (verse) → evidence (hadith) → conclusion. Learners fill each link with a quoted phrase. Grammar grows out of the chain: Learners notice that the writer adds a definition with “, which is …” and moves between the links with “As an example”, “So, in essence” and “did not …, but was …”.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses with which/that; passive voice; so and therefore.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Seeing earth, water and clay as three competing accounts: The text says they “describe both the composition and the various stages of mud”.
Turning the list of colors into a ranking, which the chapter explicitly rejects.
The claim about evolution is the chapter’s stated position; report it as “The chapter states that …” and do not open a debate beyond the text.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: non-defining clause for an added definition (mud, which is a mixture of water and soil) vs defining clause (The material from which Adam (pbuh) was created …) · formal preposition + which ↔ stranded preposition · passive for topic focus (Adam (pbuh) was created … by Allah) · As an example / So, in essence / did not …, but was ….
Notice (Activity 1): Ask “Is the sentence complete without ‘which is a mixture of water and soil’? What does the comma tell you?” Then compare the first sentence of the chapter, which has no comma.
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite “The material from which …” with the preposition at the end, turn the verse report into the passive, then complete the lines with As an example / So / but.
Likely errors: *the material which Adam was created from it · *from that Adam was created · a comma before a defining clause · Otherwise or Although in place of the conclusion or correction linker.
Use (Activity 4): a 6–8 sentence evidence-to-conclusion paragraph about a concept that can be described in more than one way (for example water as ice, liquid and steam).
content.pronunciationFocus:
A non-defining clause sits in its own tone group with a lower voice: “… the STAges of MUD, | which is a MIXture of WAter and SOIL”.
Conclusion frame with a pause: “SO, | in ESsence, | PEOple are from the SAME SOIL”.
-ed endings: created /ɪd/, expressed /t/, used /d/, evolved /d/.
Word focus: com-po-SI-tion, AN-ces-tor, SPE-cies (/ˈspiːʃiːz/), su-pe-ri-OR-i-ty, psy-cho-LOG-i-cal.
beforeReading: Show three words: earth, water, clay. Ask: “Can three different words describe one thing? When?” (for example ice / water / steam). Learners predict how the chapter will connect them.
duringReading: Underline how the chapter connects earth, water and clay.
Mark the verse example and the hadith evidence in two colors.
Box the conclusion that begins “So, in essence”.
Circle the correction “did not …, but was …”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the explanation chain in view.
Language Focus: Discover the non-defining clause in Activity 1, rewrite the relative clause and passive in Activity 2, choose the linkers in Activity 3.
Write the Activity 4 evidence-to-conclusion paragraph about a new concept.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: earth / water / clay on the board, pairs think of one thing with three names and share, one example is kept; 4–12 Listen for gist (How are the three terms connected?), then read and mark the verse and the hadith; 12–19 Explanation chain: Five cards (terms, definition, example, evidence, conclusion), pairs attach a quoted phrase to each card and check it with the class, then one learner reads the conclusion aloud and the class says which evidence supports it; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (Is the sentence complete without the which-clause?), Activities 2–3 in pairs with a two-minute board comparison of “from which” and “which … from”; 32–38 Use: Learners write the Activity 4 paragraph, partner underlines the example marker and the conclusion marker; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the chapter move from terms to a conclusion?
Why does the chapter conclude that color gives no superiority?
What is the difference between a conclusion the evidence supports and one it does not?
interactiveTips: Use the Shared Human Origin hotspot with the “So, in essence …” conclusion.
Use the Human Capacities hotspot with the final sentence about “spiritual, moral, mental, and psychological abilities”.
Ask for the sentence that licenses each conclusion before accepting it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Use four boxes (term / definition / evidence / conclusion) and the frames “____, which is ____, …” and “So, in essence, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two versions of the first sentence (formal “from which” / informal “which … from”) and explain when each is appropriate, then add a qualified conclusion to their Activity 4 paragraph.

formativeAssessment: Explains how the three terms relate.
Links the conclusion to the hadith evidence.
Distinguishes a defining from a non-defining clause and uses a conclusion marker accurately.
expectedResponses: Earth, water and clay describe the composition and stages of one material, mud; from the hadith the chapter concludes that people are from the same soil and have no superiority over one another because of their colors.
content.transferTask: Explain another concept with a definition, an example and a justified conclusion.
content.teacherReflection: Did the explanation chain make the evidence–conclusion link visible, and did learners keep diversity separate from ranking?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, attach a quoted phrase to each of the five cards: terms, definition, example, evidence, conclusion. Then one learner reads the conclusion and the class names its evidence.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (five)
What does the class name after the conclusion? (its evidence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs attach the hadith to the evidence card and not to the definition. During the board comparison, listen for learners who can say why “from which” moves the preposition. In the Use task, check the example and conclusion markers.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “, which is …” and state one conclusion with the evidence that supports it.

rubricLevels.secure: Builds the chain from terms to conclusion with a quote on each link.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the cards in order and ask only for the quotes.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells a defining from a non-defining which-clause.
rubricLevels.notYet: Cover the clause and ask “Is the sentence still complete?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses an example marker and a conclusion marker correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: List “for example / such as” and “therefore / thus” on the board.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the conclusion in proportion to the hadith evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does the hadith say more than this, or less?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter concludes from verse and hadith that shared origin gives no color any superiority. The same principle appears in modern human rights texts.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Where else have you read that people are equal whatever their color (the Farewell Sermon, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 10 of the Turkish Constitution)? How are the wordings different?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Comparing texts from different traditions is not mixing them. Learners keep each text attributed to its own source and compare only what it actually says.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
objectives: Explain why a representative needed extraordinary qualities, according to the chapter.
Separate the quoted verses (Baqarah: 31-33) from the writer’s interpretation of “the names”.
Discover how verbs of interpretation differ in strength (shows / means / refer to vs points to vs could be) and how the passive marks Adam as the one taught.
Connect knowledge with responsibility without turning a possibility into a certainty.
content.pedagogy: Make stance strength visible with a “certainty line” on the board from “certain” to “possible”. Learners place the writer’s verbs on the line and defend each position with the sentence. The quoted verses are read as a separate block and are not placed on the line because they are the source, not the interpretation. The discovery question is: “If the writer says ‘could be’, what is he not saying?”
priorKnowledge: Modal verbs of possibility; direct quotation vs commentary.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating the writer’s “could be” reading of the names as a complete, literal list.
Treating the quoted dialogue with the angels as the writer’s own interpretation.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: stance strength (… shows the value that Allah gave him / It also means … / The names refer to … vs … points to the broadness … vs … could be the fundamental knowledge …) · passive after necessity (he had to be taught by Allah) · reduced passive after a noun (The names taught to Adam (pbuh)) · reporting stance with a hedge (suggests, may).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five parts into “states directly” and “suggests a possible or partial meaning”. Ask: “Which verb is the writer most sure about? What would change if ‘could be’ became ‘is’?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct *had to taught and *The names teaching to Adam, then choose the summary that keeps the writer’s level of certainty.
Likely errors: *had to be teach · *The names teaching to Adam (the names do not teach) · reporting “could be” as “proves” or “certainly”.
Use (Activity 4): a 7–9 sentence qualified interpretation of a piece of evidence (a graph, a photo, a school result) with shows / signifies, points to and could / may.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the verses in meaning groups, calmly, with the pauses the punctuation gives: “GLOry be to YOU! | We have no KNOWledge | exCEPT what YOU have TAUGHT us.”
Weak forms: “he had to be /hæftəbi/ TAUGHT”, “could be /kədbi/ the fundaMENtal KNOWledge”.
Stress the stance verb: “POINTS to the BROADness”, “COULD be”.
Word focus: rep-re-SEN-ta-tive, ex-TRAOR-di-nar-y, fun-da-MEN-tal, civ-i-li-ZA-tion, in-TEL-li-gence.
beforeReading: Draw a “certainty line” (certain ←→ possible). Read two sentences about the school (“This result shows …” / “This result could mean …”) and ask learners where each belongs and which word decided it.
duringReading: Box the quoted verses (Baqarah: 31-33) as source text.
Underline every interpretation verb (shows, means, distinguishes, points to, could be, refer to).
Mark the two passives about teaching (had to be taught, The names taught to …).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge and label each answer as source or interpretation.
Language Focus: Sort stance in Activity 1, correct the passives in Activity 2, report the stance accurately in Activity 3.
Write the Activity 4 qualified interpretation paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Certainty line with two school sentences, learners place them and name the deciding word; 4–13 Listen and read, then a second, silent read to box the verses and underline the interpretation verbs; 13–19 Pairs place six writer phrases on the certainty line on the board (sticky notes or chalk), the class challenges any placement, verses stay off the line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (What would change if “could be” became “is”?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Each pair gets a simple evidence card (a bar chart of library use, a photo of a crowded bus), and learners write the Activity 4 paragraph moving from “shows” to “could”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer use “could be” for the content of the names?
What does the dialogue with the angels show about knowledge?
How does knowledge create responsibility rather than status?
interactiveTips: Use The Gift of Knowledge hotspot after learners have found the verse.
Use the Knowledge and Civilization hotspot with the last sentence (“science, technology, and culture”).
Do not accept a summary that turns “could be” into a fact.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a three-step ladder (shows → points to → could be) with one chapter example on each step and the frame “The chapter suggests that ____ may ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite one strong claim from their own paragraph at three levels of certainty and explain which one their evidence really supports.

formativeAssessment: Separates the quoted verses from the writer’s interpretation.
Ranks stance verbs correctly.
Uses had to be + past participle and a hedged summary.
expectedResponses: The chapter says Adam (pbuh) needed extraordinary qualities, received Allah’s spirit and had to be taught; the writer states that knowledge is the basis of science, technology and culture but only suggests that the names could be basic human knowledge.
content.transferTask: Interpret one piece of everyday evidence first with a strong and then with a cautious stance verb, and say which one is justified.
content.teacherReflection: Did the certainty line help learners hear the difference between “shows” and “could be”, and did they keep the verses separate from the commentary?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, place the six writer phrases on the certainty line on the board. Keep the verses off the line. Be ready to defend one placement.
checkQuestions: Do the verses go on the line? (no)
How many phrases do you place? (six)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Invite challenges to placements and listen for the deciding word (could, suggests, states). Check during the Use task that the paragraph moves from “shows” to “could”. Note pairs who state the names as basic human knowledge without hedging.

exitTicket: Rewrite “The names were a complete list of every science.” so that it matches the writer’s certainty.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates the quoted verses from the writer’s interpretation.
rubricLevels.notYet: Box the verses together first, then ask who wrote the rest.

rubricLevels.secure: Ranks stance verbs from strong to weak correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give “states, suggests, could be” on cards to order.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses had to be + past participle accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model sentence from the text to adapt.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a qualified paragraph that moves from fact to possibility.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “The chart shows … This could mean …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam receives 'the names' and the role of vicegerent. The writer uses 'could be' because scholars interpret the names differently.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do English academic writers show that an interpretation is one of several (may refer to, scholars differ)? Is hedging seen as weak or as honest in Turkish academic writing?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Different academic cultures hedge to different degrees. Learners notice that cautious English is a sign of precision, not of doubt.

objectives: Explain the reason the chapter gives for the higher value of Adam (pbuh) and his offspring.
Compare the functions of worldly knowledge and revelation and explain why the chapter calls them complementary.
Discover corrective contrast (not alternatives …, but rather …) and the verb patterns of need and requirement (require + person + to, necessary / essential for … to).
Identify Iblis’s refusal and the criterion he uses (“You created me from fire, and You created him from clay”).
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 separates the two parts of the chapter: An argument about two kinds of knowledge, then the quoted verses of the prostration and the refusal. Learners build a function table (what each knowledge is for) and a “reason line” for Iblis’s answer. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover that “not alternatives …, but rather …” replaces an either/or reading with a both/and reading, and that “require” and “necessary for” are followed by a to-infinitive.
priorKnowledge: Contrast with but and however; purpose with to + verb; the gift of knowledge from Chapter 3.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating worldly knowledge and revelation as rivals: The chapter says they “complete one another”.
Reading Iblis’s claim “I am better than he” as the narrator’s view: It is Iblis’s argument, which Chapter 5 answers.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: corrective contrast (These two types of knowledge are not alternatives to each other, but rather they complete one another) · require + person + to-infinitive · necessary / essential for + person + to-infinitive · However for a shift · which for a thing · through for a channel · both vs either.
Notice (Activity 1): true/false. Ask: “Does a person need one kind of knowledge or the other? Which words tell you?” Learners find that “not …, but rather …” rejects one reading and gives the correct one.
Build (Activities 2–3): correct *required even the angels prostrating and *necessary for mankind maintaining, then complete the lines with However / which / through / both.
Likely errors: *required the angels prostrating · *necessary for mankind maintaining · who for revelation · either instead of both.
Use (Activity 4): a 7–9 sentence complementarity argument about two resources or skills (for example reading and discussion, practice and theory).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress: “NOT alTERnatives to each OTHer, | but RAther they comPLETE one aNOTHer”.
Keep “both” strong and “to” weak: “need BOTH types”, “necessary for MANkind to /tə/ mainTAIN …”.
Read the quoted verses in calm meaning groups, without drama: “They BOWED DOWN, | exCEPT for SAtan.”
Word focus: rev-e-LA-tion, es-SEN-tial, PRIV-i-lege, OFF-spring, AR-ro-gant, al-TER-na-tives.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can two things be different and still need each other? Give an example.” (a map and a compass, a doctor and a patient’s description). Learners predict what two kinds of knowledge the chapter might compare.
duringReading: Mark the reason given for the value of Adam (pbuh) and his offspring.
Build a two-column table: Worldly knowledge / revelation, each with its function in the text’s words.
Underline “not alternatives …, but rather …”.
In the verses, mark who refuses and the reason he gives.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and write a bridge note: One function of each kind of knowledge.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on corrective contrast, verb patterns of need and the shift to revelation (Activities 1–3).
Write the Activity 4 complementarity argument about a new context.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: “different but needing each other”, pairs give one example and predict the two kinds of knowledge; 5–14 Listen and read the first two paragraphs, then the verses separately with the audio; 14–24 Function table in pairs: Worldly knowledge (to maintain worldly life) / revelation (to understand role, duty and order), each cell with a quoted phrase, then a whole-class check; 24–31 Reason line in groups of three: command → the angels bow down → Iblis refuses → his stated reason (fire / clay), learners label the reason “Iblis’s claim”, not the narrator’s; 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note: One function of each kind of knowledge; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the function table orally; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as discovery (one or the other, or both?), learners rephrase the rule in their own words; 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then a board line “require someone to / necessary for someone to” built from their corrections; 22–33 Use: The Activity 4 argument about two complementary skills, with “not … but rather” in the middle; 33–38 Pairs swap and underline where the either/or reading is rejected; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the chapter say the two kinds of knowledge are not alternatives?
What job does each kind of knowledge do?
What criterion does Iblis use to claim he is better, and what does it leave out?
interactiveTips: Use the Two Forms of Knowledge hotspot for the function table.
Use the Iblis’s Arrogance hotspot only after learners have found his stated reason in the verse.
Keep the verses as read-and-explain text; do not gap or rewrite them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two-column table with one cell filled and the frames “____ is necessary for us to ____.” and “They are not alternatives, but rather ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Add a paragraph showing how two different resources serve one shared goal, using both “require … to” and “essential for … to”.

formativeAssessment: Names a distinct function for each kind of knowledge.
Explains the either/or vs both/and difference.
Uses require / necessary for + to-infinitive accurately.
expectedResponses: The chapter gives knowledge as the reason for human value, presents worldly knowledge and revelation as complementary (one for worldly life, one for role and duty), and shows Iblis refusing to prostrate because he claims fire is better than clay.
content.transferTask: Explain two complementary resources in school or daily life, showing the job of each and the goal they share.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the both/and meaning of “not …, but rather …” themselves, and did they keep Iblis’s claim separate from the narrator’s view?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, fill the function table for worldly knowledge and revelation with a quoted phrase in each cell. Then, in groups of three, build the reason line and label Iblis’s reason as his claim.
checkQuestions: How do you label Iblis’s reason? (as his claim, not the narrator’s)
How many kinds of knowledge are in the table? (two)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that groups label the fire and clay reason as Iblis’s claim. In Lesson 2, build the board line from the learners’ own corrections. In the Use task, look for “not … but rather” in the middle of the argument.

exitTicket: Complete: “They are not alternatives to each other, but rather ____. One is necessary for us to ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Names a different function for each kind of knowledge with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the two phrases in the text that give each function.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains “not alternatives … but rather complete one another”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Do we choose one, or do we need both?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses require someone to and necessary for someone to accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the board line as a model to copy.

rubricLevels.secure: Argues that two skills complete each other.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “X is not an alternative to Y, but rather …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter calls worldly knowledge and revelation complementary, not alternatives. Ideas about science and faith are discussed differently in different societies.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In which countries or periods did scholars work on both kinds of knowledge (Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Ibn Sina, Andalusian scholars)? How is the relation discussed in English-speaking schools today?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Keep the discussion on what the chapter claims. Learners should not be asked to defend or attack anyone's beliefs; they explain the chapter's view in clear English.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
objectives: Explain the prostration as obedience to Allah and respect for Adam (pbuh), not worship.
Analyse Iblis’s criterion (origin) and the evidence the chapter sets against it.
Discover how clarification markers (which is, in other words, that is), reason markers (because, since) and contrast markers (On the other hand, yet) organize an argument.
Reject superiority based on race, color or ethnicity, as the chapter does.
content.pedagogy: Turn the chapter into an argument map: Claim (Iblis: my origin is superior) → reason (the material he was created from) → counter-evidence (Adam’s humble origin) → principle (Allah does not focus on origins). Learners place quoted phrases on the map. The language work grows out of it: Learners discover that the map’s arrows are the linkers in the text (because, since, yet, On the other hand) and that “that is” and “in other words” make key words precise.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 4’s refusal scene; because and although.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating the prostration as worship of Adam: The text says “such prostration is solely to and for Allah”.
Accepting Iblis’s criterion as a reasonable standard because it is stated confidently.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: clarification (which is faith or Islam / in other words, Iblis’ / that is, race, color, or ethnicity) · reason (because …, since all humans ultimately originate from dried mud) · contrasting view or counter-evidence (On the other hand, … / …, yet Adam (pbuh)’s humble origin shows …) · X, yet Y ↔ Although X, Y · Y because X ↔ X, therefore Y.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match four expressions with what they clarify. Ask: “Which one gives a second name for the same being? Which one makes the word ‘origins’ concrete?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the yet-sentence with Although and the because-sentence with therefore, then sort “gives a reason” / “introduces a contrasting view”.
Likely errors: *Although …, yet … (double marker) · *because of + clause · therefore in front of the cause · “that is” used to add a new idea instead of clarifying.
Use (Activity 4): a 6–8 sentence paragraph challenging a weak criterion (for example judging a book by its cover, a player only by height).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Clarifications are said on a lower pitch between pauses: “SAtan’s | — in OTHer words, IBlis’ — | unaPPARent ARrogance …”, “ORigins, | THAT is, | RACE, Color, or ethNICity”.
Stress the turn: “On the OTHer HAND, |”, “… , YET ADam’s HUMble ORigin …”.
Word focus: in-a-BIL-i-ty, o-BE-di-ence, ad-mi-RA-tion, eth-NIC-i-ty, un-ap-PAR-ent.
beforeReading: Show a harmless weak criterion: “The best student is the one with the most expensive pen.” Ask: “What is wrong with this criterion? What evidence would you use against it?”
duringReading: Find the sentence that says the prostration is not worship and the reason given.
Mark Iblis’s claim and the reason behind it.
Underline the counter-evidence introduced by “yet”.
Circle every “which is”, “in other words” and “that is”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Match the clarifications in Activity 1, recombine cause and contrast in Activity 2, sort reason vs contrasting view in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 paragraph challenging a weak criterion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: The “expensive pen” criterion, pairs say why it is weak; 4–12 Listen and read, then find the not-worship sentence and its reason; 12–19 Argument map in groups of four on A3 paper: claim / reason / counter-evidence / principle, each with a quoted phrase and the linker that joins it, one map is checked under the visualiser or on the board; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (second name or concrete meaning?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, learners explain why “Although … yet” is wrong; 31–38 Use: Each group chooses a weak everyday criterion and writes the Activity 4 paragraph, one group reads and the class names the counter-evidence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is the prostration described as obedience and respect rather than worship?
What evidence does the chapter set against Iblis’s criterion?
What does it mean that Allah “does not focus on origins”?
interactiveTips: Use the Knowledge and Obedience hotspot with the first paragraph.
Use the False Superiority hotspot with the “yet” sentence and the principle about origins.
Do not allow origin, race or color to become ranking language in examples.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four boxes of the argument map with the linkers printed on the arrows and the frame “Although ____, ____ shows that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the same argument twice, once with “yet” and once with “Although”, and explain which version puts more weight on the counter-evidence.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the prostration is not worship.
Identifies Iblis’s criterion and the counter-evidence.
Uses clarification, reason and contrast markers accurately.
expectedResponses: The prostration is obedience to Allah that shows respect to Adam (pbuh); Iblis bases his superiority on the material he was created from, yet Adam’s humble origin shows that Allah does not focus on race, color or ethnicity.
content.transferTask: Challenge one weak everyday criterion with evidence and state a better criterion.
content.teacherReflection: Did the argument map help learners see linkers as the logic of the text, and did they separate Iblis’s reasoning from the chapter’s evaluation?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of four, make an argument map on A3 paper: claim, reason, counter-evidence and principle. Write a quoted phrase and the joining linker in each box.
checkQuestions: How many boxes? (four)
What else goes in each box besides the phrase? (the linker)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Give roles: reader, writer, checker, presenter. Check that the counter-evidence box uses Adam’s humble origin from the text. Listen in Activity 3 for learners who explain why “Although … yet” is wrong.

exitTicket: Name the weak criterion in the chapter and write one sentence with “yet” that introduces the counter-evidence.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the prostration is respect and obedience, not worship.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the not-worship sentence and its reason.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses clarification markers such as “that is” or “in other words”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give two markers to choose from in a gap sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses reason and contrast markers without doubling them.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Do we need both Although and yet?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Shows why a weak criterion such as an expensive pen is unfair.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “This criterion is weak because …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The prostration is explained as respect, not worship. Bowing has very different meanings across cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What does bowing mean in Japan (a greeting), in a British court (respect for the judge) and in Islamic worship (sujud only for Allah)? Why does the chapter need to explain the angels' prostration?
interculturalFocus.perspective: A gesture cannot be understood without its culture. Learners avoid judging a foreign gesture until they know its meaning there.

objectives: Distinguish what the verse allows, what it forbids and why (A’raf, verse 19).
Contrast the two paths described by the narrator (Satan’s and Adam’s).
Discover how imperatives permit, command and forbid, how “while” sets two paths side by side, and how “will” states a firm intention.
Explain how Satan’s declared intention shapes what the reader expects next.
content.pedagogy: The chapter mixes verses and narrator sentences. Learners first sort every line into “verse” or “narrator” so the source is always clear. Then they build a “freedom and limit” diagram from verse 19: a big circle (inhabit, eat whatever you wish) with one small forbidden point (this tree). The language is discovered from the speech acts: Learners notice that the same imperative form can open freedom or set a limit, and that “I will surely …” is not a prediction but a declared intention.
priorKnowledge: Imperatives; will for future; while for time.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reading the command as a ban on everything: the verse gives wide freedom and one limit.
Reading “will” in Satan’s words as a neutral prediction rather than a declared intention made with an oath.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: imperatives that permit, command and forbid (inhabit the Garden, eat whatever you wish, do not approach this tree) · for fear that + clause for a warning · a request with a time limit (Lord, allow me until the Day they are raised up) · while = whereas · by + -ing for means ↔ because / when + clause · will for firm intention (I will surely sit in wait …, By Your majesty, I will deceive them all).
Notice (Activity 1): matching. Ask: “Which line opens a wide freedom, and which line sets one limit inside it? Which line is a request?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the narrator’s while-sentence with whereas and the by-phrase as a clause, then decide what “will” expresses in Satan’s words.
Likely errors: *Don’t to approach · *while he reached …, but … · *by challenge · reading “will” as a neutral prediction.
Use (Activity 4): a 7–9 sentence paragraph about two people or courses of action moving in different directions, with one boundary, one while-contrast and two “will” forms of intention.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Balance the two halves of the narrator’s contrast: “WHILE SAtan reached the POINT of no reTURN | … , ADam took a PATH completely DIFFerent from him”.
Intention is stressed on the auxiliary: “I WILL SUREly SIT in WAIT”, “I WILL deCEIVE them ALL”.
Read the verses in calm meaning groups; do not dramatise Satan’s words.
Word focus: in-HAB-it, WRONG-do-ers, OUT-cast, de-CEIVE, re-SPECT-ful, MAJ-es-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “If you are given almost complete freedom and only one rule, what does that rule tell you?” Learners give one school example (you may use the library freely, but not …).
duringReading: Label each paragraph: verse or narrator.
In verse 19, mark what is allowed, what is forbidden and the reason given.
Underline the narrator’s while-sentence.
Circle every “will” in Satan’s words.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Match the lines to speech acts in Activity 1, rewrite the contrast in Activity 2, decide what “will” expresses in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 two-paths paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: one freedom, one rule, learners give a school example; 4–11 Listen and read, then label each paragraph verse / narrator; 11–18 Freedom-and-limit diagram in pairs from verse 19 (big circle: inhabit, eat whatever you wish / one point: this tree / arrow: for fear that you become wrongdoers), then a T-chart of the two paths from the narrator’s sentence; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (freedom, limit or request?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 as a whole-class vote with justification (prediction or intention?); 31–38 Use: Activity 4 paragraph about two classmates’ different study plans or two possible school projects, with “will” for intention, partner checks the “while” sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the single limit in a wide freedom teach?
How do the narrator’s two paths differ?
Why does “By Your majesty, I will …” sound like a vow rather than a forecast?
interactiveTips: Use the Life in Paradise hotspot with verse 19 and the sentence “he had his wife with him”.
Use the Satan’s Vow hotspot with the “I will …” lines.
Replay the verses only to inspect meaning and speech act; never ask learners to perform Satan’s words.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the five lines of Activity 1 on cards with the labels allow / command / forbid / warn / request, and the frame “While ____, ____ took a different path.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two versions of one intention (with “will” and with “be going to”) and explain which sounds more like a firm promise and why.

formativeAssessment: Separates verse and narrator.
Identifies the allowed, the forbidden and the warning.
Explains “will” as intention and uses while / whereas accurately.
expectedResponses: Adam (pbuh) and his wife may live in the Garden and eat whatever they wish but must not approach the tree; Satan, who reached the point of no return, declares with an oath that he will deceive them, while Adam takes a completely different path.
content.transferTask: Describe one set of rules you know that gives wide freedom with one clear limit, and explain the reason for the limit.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep verse and narrator separate, and did they discover that one imperative form can permit or forbid?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw the freedom-and-limit diagram from verse 19: a big circle for what is allowed, one point for the tree and an arrow for the warning. Then make a T-chart of the two paths.
checkQuestions: What goes on the one point? (the tree)
What does the arrow show? (the warning)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs label each paragraph verse or narrator before drawing. During the class vote on Activity 3, ask voters to justify prediction or intention. In the Use task, check the while sentence for a real contrast.

exitTicket: Write one sentence that gives freedom with a limit and one “will” sentence that states a firm intention.

rubricLevels.secure: Labels each paragraph as verse or narrator.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read one paragraph and ask “Who is speaking here?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Identifies what is allowed, what is forbidden and the warning.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask three questions: may, must not, for fear that.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses while and whereas for two different paths.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Satan …, while Adam …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains “will” here as intention, not prediction.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is Satan guessing, or is he deciding?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Wide freedom with one clear limit is the pattern of the Paradise command. Rules of this kind exist in every society.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which places in Türkiye have wide freedom and one firm rule (a mosque courtyard: no shoes inside; a library: silence)? Name a similar rule in a museum or park abroad.
interculturalFocus.perspective: Visitors often break rules they did not know. Learners write one polite English sign that explains a local rule to a visitor, with its reason.

objectives: Trace the chain from human vulnerability through repeated persuasion and uncertainty to the decision and its consequence.
Explain how Satan presents himself (“I am a sincere advisor to you”) and why this is deception.
Discover how the writer moves between a general truth (present simple) and story events (past), and how conditionals, might and the past perfect organize uncertainty and sequence.
Keep both human vulnerability and human responsibility in view.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds a six-step persuasion chain from the text (vulnerability → motive → repeated whispering → false promise → uncertainty → decision → consequence), each step with a quoted phrase. Learners notice that nothing is forced: Every step is persuasion. Lesson 2 asks why the writer suddenly switches to the present in a past story: Learners discover that “man tends to forget” is a general truth that explains the events, then work on no sooner, if, might and had warned.
priorKnowledge: The prohibition and Satan’s vow in Chapter 6; past simple and past perfect.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Saying Satan forced Adam and Eve: The text shows whispering, a promise and an oath, not force.
Treating Adam’s “It might truly be …” as certainty rather than doubt.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present simple for a general truth inside a past narrative (man tends to forget / His heart changes / his determination weakens) · participle clause (…, trying to persuade both) · As soon as + past perfect ↔ No sooner had … than … · first conditional (What will happen if I eat from this tree?) · might for uncertainty · past perfect for the earlier event (They forgot that Allah had warned them …).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts into “true of people in general” and “one event in this story”. Ask: “Why does the writer switch to the present in a story about the past? Is ‘man tends to forget’ only about Adam?”
Build (Activities 2–3): expand the participle clause (and he was trying to …) and rewrite “As soon as …” with No sooner had …, then choose eat / might / had warned.
Likely errors: *if I will eat · *It must truly be (certainty) · *They forgot that Allah warned / has warned · *No sooner Adam had finished.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph about someone gradually persuaded into a poor decision, moving from a general tendency to a specific case.
content.pronunciationFocus:
General truths are read with a steady, falling tune: “MAN TENDS to forGET. | His HEART CHANges, | and his deterMInation WEAKens.”
-s and -ed endings: tends /z/, changes /ɪz/, weakens /z/ / whispered /d/, picked /t/, offered /d/, decided /ɪd/, finished /t/, ceased /t/.
Doubt has a rising, uncertain tune: “It MIGHT TRUly be …?”
Word focus: de-ter-mi-NA-tion, im-MOR-tals, sin-CERE, pre-OC-cu-pied, ma-NIP-u-late.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can someone be persuaded without being forced?” Pairs list two techniques (repeating, flattering, promising) from advertising or social media.
duringReading: Mark the three present-simple statements about people.
Underline Satan’s promise and his oath.
Mark Adam’s question and his “might”.
Number the final events: decided → stretched out his hand → offered → ate → felt.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and write a bridge note: One vulnerability and one persuasive move.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on general truth vs story event, participle and no sooner, condition, possibility and earlier past (Activities 1–3).
Write or say the Activity 4 vulnerability–decision–consequence paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: Persuasion without force, pairs list two techniques from advertising; 5–15 Listen with books closed (What does Satan promise?), then read along; 15–26 Persuasion chain in groups of four: Six strips (vulnerability, motive, whispering, promise and oath, doubt, decision) placed in order, each with a quoted phrase, groups compare with the next group; 26–32 Responsibility check: Learners find evidence that Adam and Eve made a decision (“they decided”, “They forgot …”) and write one balanced sentence (vulnerable but responsible); 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the chain from memory; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as discovery (Why the present in a past story?), learners state the rule in their own words; 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then a board timeline showing “had warned” before “forgot”; 22–33 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a harmless case (a student persuaded to skip revision, a buyer persuaded by an advert); 33–38 Peer check: Underline the general truth, the “if” clause and the “might”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which human tendencies does the writer name, and how do they explain the events?
Why does a promise of sincere advice make persuasion stronger?
How does the text keep both vulnerability and responsibility?
interactiveTips: Use the Weakening Determination hotspot with the present-simple sentences.
Use The Forbidden Tree hotspot with the decision and its immediate consequence.
Read the quoted verses as source text; learners explain them but do not rewrite them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give five boxes (tendency / promise / doubt / decision / consequence) and the frames “People tend to ____.”, “What will happen if ____?”, “It might ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph that shows vulnerability without removing responsibility, using “No sooner had … than …” once.

formativeAssessment: Builds the persuasion chain with evidence.
Explains the general-truth present.
Uses if + present, might and the past perfect accurately.
expectedResponses: The chapter shows Satan using Adam’s human forgetfulness and weakening determination, whispering day after day and swearing he is a sincere advisor; Adam wonders if the tree might be the Tree of Immortality, they decide to eat, and as soon as he has eaten he feels pain, sadness and shame.
content.transferTask: Analyse a harmless persuasive message (an advert or a social-media post): its promise, its evidence and what it leaves out.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover why the present simple appears in a past narrative, and did they keep vulnerability and responsibility together?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In groups of four, put the six persuasion strips in order. Back each strip with a quoted phrase, then compare your chain with the next group.
checkQuestions: How many strips? (six)
Who do you compare with? (the next group)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the decision strip comes last and that groups find “they decided”. In the responsibility check, listen for a balanced sentence: vulnerable but responsible. In Lesson 2, look for the board timeline with “had warned” before “forgot”.

exitTicket: Write one general truth in the present simple and one sentence with “No sooner had … than …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Builds the persuasion chain in order with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last strips.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the present tense for a general truth inside a past story.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this true only then, or always?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses if + present, might and the past perfect accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model sentence for each form from the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a balanced sentence: vulnerable but responsible.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Although they were …, they still …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Satan presents himself as a 'sincere advisor'. Persuasion techniques work across cultures and languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Compare a Turkish and an English advert for the same kind of product. Which promise words appear in each (best, guaranteed, sağlıklı, doğal)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that advertising language travels through translation. They analyse the technique, not the people of either culture.

objectives: Explain the immediate reaction of Adam (pbuh) and Eve and the reason the chapter gives for it (haya).
Interpret the dialogue: What Allah’s questions do and what Adam’s reply means.
Discover the time → result → reason chain (When, so, because) and how the last paragraph separates what the Qur’an says from what scholars add.
Keep what the Qur’an does not describe (the tree) as unknown.
content.pedagogy: Use three “source levels” on the board: What the Qur’an says / what it does not say / what scholars add. Learners place the last paragraph’s sentences on the levels. Before that, they analyse the dialogue as speech acts: You ask “Does Allah ask ‘Did I not forbid you …?’ to get information?” and learners discover that a negative question can remind. The discovery of the chain When → so → because comes from the narrator’s second paragraph.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 7’s decision; because and so; according to.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Inventing the type of tree: The chapter says “This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an.”
Presenting the scholars’ timing (“before he became a prophet”) as Qur’anic wording.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: negative question as a reminder (Did I not forbid you from this tree …?) · a question that tests meaning (Are you running away from Me?) · No, …, but … (No, my Lord, but I am shy of You.) · time → result → reason (When they tasted the fruit … , so they both started … because the sense of shame (haya) is inborn human nature …) · source marking (This tree is not described in … / It is only mentioned that … / According to Islamic scholars, … / that is, …).
Notice (Activity 1): matching. Ask: “Does Allah ask ‘Did I not forbid you …?’ to learn something new? What does the question do?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the narrator’s lines with When / so / because, then sort “what the Qur’an says or does not say” and “an interpretation added by others”.
Likely errors: So used for a reason and because for a result · *because of + clause · dropping “According to Islamic scholars” in a summary.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence source-aware paragraph about a historical, scientific or cultural claim: What the source says, what it does not specify, what a researcher adds, one “that is”, one reminding question answered with “No, …, but …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
A reminding question falls at the end: “Did I NOT forBID you from this TREE …↘”.
Correction with a pause: “NO, my LORD, | but I am SHY of You.”
The repeated plea is short and urgent but not theatrical: “FORgiveness! | FORgiveness!”
Word focus: de-CEP-tion, EV-i-dent, un-CLAD, for-BID-den, ha-YÂ (/ħaˈjaː/, “ha-YAA”).
beforeReading: Ask: “When a teacher asks ‘Didn’t I tell you to bring your book?’, does she want information?” Learners say what the question really does.
duringReading: Mark the immediate action and the reason for it.
Label each line of dialogue: reminds / tests meaning / rejects and replaces / pleads.
In the last paragraph, mark what is not described and what is attributed to scholars.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge and answer before revealing the evidence.
Language Focus: Match the dialogue lines in Activity 1, complete the time–result–reason chain in Activity 2, sort text vs interpretation in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 source-aware paragraph about a new claim.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “Didn’t I tell you …?” learners say what the question does; 4–12 Listen and read, then mark the immediate action and its reason; 12–18 Source levels on the board: Pairs place the four last-paragraph sentences under says / does not say / scholars add, two pairs explain a placement; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (information or reminder?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners retell the chain aloud: when → so → because; 31–38 Use: Learners choose a claim from science or history class (for example who built a monument) and write the Activity 4 paragraph with three source levels, partner checks that no attributed view became a fact; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the immediate covering show, according to the chapter?
Why does Adam answer “No, … but …”?
Why does admitting what a source does not say make writing more trustworthy?
interactiveTips: Use the Recognition and Modesty hotspot with the haya sentence.
Use the Turning Back to Allah hotspot with “Forgiveness! Forgiveness!” and Adam’s reply.
Keep the three source levels visible on the board for the whole lesson.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give labels (the source says / the source does not say / according to …) and the frame “When ____, ____, so ____ because ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Correct an overconfident paragraph (prepared by you about a school topic) by restoring the source boundaries.

formativeAssessment: Explains the reason for the reaction (haya).
Identifies the function of each question.
Keeps Qur’anic wording, omission and scholarly interpretation separate.
expectedResponses: After eating, they saw their nakedness and covered themselves at once because shame (haya) is inborn human nature; Adam cried for forgiveness and said he was shy of his Lord, and the chapter notes that the tree is not described in the Qur’an while the timing is given “according to Islamic scholars”.
content.transferTask: Write one set of three sentences about a claim you know: What the source says, what it does not say and what someone else interprets.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the reminding function of the negative question, and did they keep scholarly interpretation separate from the Qur’anic text?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, place the four sentences of the last paragraph under three headings on the board: the Qur’an says, the Qur’an does not say, scholars add.
checkQuestions: How many headings? (three)
Where does a scholar’s view go? (under scholars add)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Ask two pairs to explain a placement and listen for “according to Islamic scholars” as their evidence. In the Use task, check that no attributed view has become a plain fact.

exitTicket: Write one statement the Qur’an does not make about the tree and one sentence starting “According to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the text’s reason for their reaction: haya.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence with “because” and ask what it explains.

rubricLevels.secure: Says whether each question informs or reminds.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did they know the answer already?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps Qur’anic wording, omission and scholarly view at separate levels.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three headings with one example under each.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a connected paragraph with three source levels.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frames “The source says … / It does not say … / Some experts add …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam and Eve feel haya, translated in the chapter as shame and modesty. English has no single word that matches haya or Turkish 'hayâ / utanma'.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English words are near (shame, modesty, embarrassment, self-respect) and how is each different? Which one would you use to explain hayâ to a visitor?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Some concepts are culture-specific. Learners explain the idea with a short definition and an example instead of forcing a single-word translation.

objectives: Trace repentance as regret → turning to Allah → prayer → words received → forgiveness → descent → prophethood.
Explain the meaning of “Unless You forgive us …” in the prayer.
Discover “unless” as “if … not”, cause as a noun (the reason for / because of), active vs passive, the past perfect, neither … nor, and must + base verb.
Distinguish what humans are capable of (sinning) from what they must do (recognize, seek the fault, turn back).
content.pedagogy: Build a “recovery path” on the board: The steps from regret to a new direction, each with a quoted phrase. Learners notice that the path does not stop at regret. The language discovery begins with the prayer: You ask “What happens if there is no forgiveness? Which word carries ‘if … not’?” Then learners compare how the chapter describes what humans are open to and what they must do.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 8’s cry for forgiveness; if-clauses; modal must.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating regret alone as complete repentance: The text adds turning to Allah, prayer and changed direction.
Reading the descent as a punishment only: The chapter stresses forgiveness first (Chapter 10 will reframe the descent).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: unless = if … not (Unless You forgive us, and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.) · cause as subject vs cause after a preposition (His regret itself was the reason for Allah’s mercy upon him ↔ … because of his regret) · passive ↔ active (was forgiven by Allah ↔ Allah forgave …) · past perfect (what he had done) · neither … nor · must + base verb controlling three verbs (must recognize …, seek …, and immediately turn …).
Notice (Activity 1): Ask “What happens if there is no forgiveness? Which sentence says the same thing with ‘if’?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the cause with because of / due to and the passive as an active, then correct *has done, *neither … or and *must to recognize.
Likely errors: *Unless You don’t forgive us (double negative) · *what he has done · *neither a community or a congregation · *must to recognize.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence responsibility-and-recovery paragraph about a non-story mistake, ending with a concrete change of direction.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep the condition in one tone group: “unLESS You forGIVE us, | and have MERcy on us, | we will be aMONG the LOsers.”
Parallel stress: “NEIther a comMUnity | NOR a congreGAtion”.
-ed endings: regretted /ɪd/, turned /d/, pardoned /d/, descended /ɪd/, committed /ɪd/.
Word focus: re-PENT-ance, PROPH-et-hood, con-gre-GA-tion, un-in-TEN-tion-al, HON-oured (silent h).
beforeReading: Ask: “After you realize you made a mistake, what has to happen before things are really better?” Pairs list three steps and keep them for comparison.
duringReading: Mark each step of the recovery path.
Underline the prayer and circle “Unless”.
Box the passive sentence about the mistake being forgiven.
Mark what humans are “open to” and what they “must” do.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Interpret “unless” in Activity 1, rewrite cause and passive in Activity 2, correct the three forms in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 responsibility-and-recovery paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Three steps after a mistake, pairs list them; 4–12 Listen and read, then compare their three steps with the chapter; 12–18 Recovery path: Seven step-cards in mixed order, pairs sequence them with a quoted phrase for each, then the class agrees on where the path ends (prophethood and a responsible direction, not just regret); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (What happens without forgiveness?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners make one “unless” sentence about class rules; 31–38 Use: Activity 4 paragraph about a non-story mistake (a group project deadline missed, a damaged library book), partner checks that it ends with changed action; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is regret the start of repentance but not the end?
What does “Unless You forgive us …” show about dependence on Allah?
What is the difference between “humans are open to sinning” and “they must recognize their mistakes”?
interactiveTips: Use the Repentance Accepted hotspot with the prayer and the forgiveness sentence.
Use the Life on Earth hotspot with the descent and the later prophethood.
Read the prayer as source text; learners explain “unless” but do not rewrite the verse.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give recognition / condition / obligation / action boxes and the frames “Unless ____, ____.” and “In order to ____, we must ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Compare Adam’s regret here with Qabil’s regret in Chapter 15 after reading it, or write a paragraph with two different “unless” conditions.

formativeAssessment: Sequences the recovery path.
Paraphrases “unless” correctly.
Uses the past perfect, neither … nor and must + base verb accurately.
expectedResponses: Adam severely regretted what he had done and turned to Allah; the prayer says that unless Allah forgives them they will be among the losers; Allah taught him how to ask for forgiveness and forgave him, and later, when a community emerged, he was given prophethood.
content.transferTask: Write a repair plan for a harmless mistake using one “unless” condition, one cause and one “must”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the meaning of “unless” from the prayer, and did they move beyond emotion to responsible action in their writing?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, put the seven step-cards in order and add a quoted phrase to each. Then agree with the class where the path ends.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (seven)
Does the path end with regret? (no, with prophethood and a responsible direction)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for pairs who stop the path at regret and ask what comes after. In the class-rules round, check that each unless sentence keeps a positive meaning. In the Use task, check that each paragraph ends with a changed action.

exitTicket: Write one “unless” sentence and name the step that makes recovery more than regret.

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the recovery steps in order with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Paraphrases unless as “if … not” correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Rewrite one unless sentence with “if … not” together.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses the past perfect, neither … nor and must + base verb accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Ends the paragraph with a concrete changed action.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What will you do differently next time?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The prayer 'Unless You forgive us …' expresses dependence and hope. Apology to people and repentance to Allah are expressed differently in different languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English phrases express regret formally (I deeply regret, I sincerely apologise)? Which Turkish phrases do the same (Pişmanım, Affınıza sığınırım)? What level of formality does each carry?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Formal regret can sound cold in English and very warm in Turkish. Learners compare tone, not sincerity.

objectives: Explain how the chapter reframes the descent: Not “dishonor or humiliation” but “an honorable and respected settlement”.
Explain the purpose the chapter gives for the experience (It was meant to teach …).
Discover how the chapter separates named sources (Ibn Abbas said, Ibn Umar said) from unnamed reports (It is also reported that …, It is said to …), and how “would” looks forward from a past moment.
Report the place of descent without turning any report into a certain fact.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 separates the two halves of the chapter: An interpretation of the descent, then several reports about its place. Learners build a “source ladder” for the reports (named narrator in direct speech → named narrator in reported speech → impersonal report), and a reframing box for “not … but rather …”. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover what “would” does after “knew” and how impersonal passives keep distance between writer and claim.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 9’s descent; reporting verbs; future with will.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating all reported locations as equally certain facts.
Reading the descent only as humiliation, which the chapter explicitly rejects.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: named vs unnamed source (Ibn Abbas, who narrated many hadiths, said: “…” / Ibn Umar said that … vs It is also reported that … / It is said to have come from Paradise) · would as future in the past (Allah knew that Adam (pbuh) and Eve would eat of the tree …) · was meant to + base verb for purpose · did not + base verb …, but rather … (did not imply dishonor or humiliation, but rather it was …).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five reports into “a named person is the source” and “no source is named”. Ask: “Who says Adam descended on land ‘Dihna’? Who says he descended with the Black Stone? What does the writer gain by not naming a source?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Decide what “would” shows after “knew”, then correct *will violate, *was meant to teaching and *did not implied.
Likely errors: *He knew that Satan will violate … · *was meant to teaching · *did not implied · summarising “It is said to have come from Paradise” as “It came from Paradise”.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph about a non-story event with more than one account, using would, was meant to, not … but rather … and two different source frames.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Weak “would” and “that” in reported future: “alLAH KNEW that /ðət/ ADam and EVE would /wəd/ EAT of the TREE”.
Source frames as single chunks with a pause: “It is ALso rePORTed that | …”, “It is SAID to have COME from PARadise”.
Corrective contrast: “did NOT imPLY dishonor | but RAther …”.
Word focus: vice-GER-en-cy, hu-mil-i-A-tion, COR-ner-stone, PIL-grim-age, IN-no-cence.
beforeReading: Tell learners: “Three friends describe where the school trip bus stopped, and they disagree. Is the trip itself still certain?” Collect how to report the three versions fairly.
duringReading: Mark the purpose sentence (It was meant to teach …).
Underline the reframing “not … but rather …”.
Number the four location reports and label each: Named direct / named reported / unnamed.
Circle “would” after “knew”.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and leave a bridge note: One core claim and one qualified report.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on source frames, future in the past and purpose/correction (Activities 1–3).
Write or say the Activity 4 multi-account paragraph and audit its certainty.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: Three versions of the bus stop, how do we report them fairly?; 5–14 Listen and read, then a second reading of the first two paragraphs only; 14–22 Reframing box in pairs: What the descent is not / what it is / what it was meant to teach, each with a quoted phrase; 22–31 Source ladder in groups of three: Four report cards placed on three rungs (named direct, named reported, unnamed), groups justify each placement with the frame word; 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the ladder orally; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 (confirms the ladder), then Activity 2 as discovery (What does “would” show after “knew”?), with a timeline on the board; 12–20 Activity 3 in pairs, then learners explain each correction to a partner; 20–32 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a local event people remember differently (a school founding, a festival, a match), with two source frames; 32–37 Certainty audit: Partners mark any reported detail written as a plain fact and rewrite it; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the chapter insist the descent was not humiliation?
Why is “It is said to …” different from a direct assertion?
What does the experience teach, according to the chapter?
interactiveTips: Use the A Responsible Settlement hotspot with the reframing and purpose sentences.
Use the Places of Descent hotspot with the source ladder, not as a memorisation task.
Keep each source frame attached to the claim it qualifies.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give labels (named person said / it is reported / it is said) and the frames “____ knew that ____ would ____.” and “It was not ____, but rather ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite one claim at three levels of certainty (asserted / attributed to a named person / impersonally reported) and explain the effect of each.

formativeAssessment: Explains the reframing of the descent.
Classifies every report by source type.
Uses would, was meant to and did not + base verb accurately.
expectedResponses: The chapter presents the descent as an honorable settlement meant to teach that Satan is the enemy and that the right path is to follow the Creator; it gives the place through named narrators (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar) and unnamed reports, keeping each at its own level of certainty.
content.transferTask: Rewrite an overconfident claim about a local event with the right source frame.
content.teacherReflection: Did the source ladder help learners keep reported details at a distance, and did they discover the future-in-the-past meaning of “would” themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, complete the reframing box. Then, in groups of three, place the four report cards on the three rungs of the source ladder and justify each place with the frame word.
checkQuestions: How many rungs on the ladder? (three)
What do you use to justify a place? (the frame word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that named narrators (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar) are on different rungs from unnamed reports. In Lesson 2, partners should explain each correction aloud. During the certainty audit, check that learners rewrite reported details with a frame.

rubric: Future in the past and purpose
exitTicket: Write one core claim about the chapter and one detail with “It is reported that …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what the descent is, what it is not and what it teaches.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the three phrases in the first paragraphs.

rubricLevels.secure: Places each report on the right source level.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame words “said”, “it is reported”, “some say”.

rubricLevels.criterion: Future in the past and purpose
rubricLevels.secure: Uses would after knew, was meant to and did not + base verb accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Draw the timeline and place “would” on it.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps reported details at their level of certainty.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who said this? How sure can we be?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter separates named sources (Ibn Abbas said) from unnamed reports (It is said …). Report verbs carry different weight in English academic culture.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How does a Turkish newspaper mark a rumour (iddia edildi, söylendi)? How does an English newspaper do it (allegedly, reportedly, it is claimed)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners see that careful reporting is a shared value. They rewrite one local news claim in English with the right report verb.

objectives: Identify the responsibilities Adam (pbuh) had on Earth: practical, moral and social.
Explain the chapter’s claim about removing Allah from the human mind.
Discover how the chapter compresses time (No sooner had one ended than another began), repeats necessity (had to), ranks priority (Above all) and states a wider consequence (means).
Connect stewardship of the Earth with concrete responsibility today.
content.pedagogy: Learners build a “responsibility web” with Adam in the center and every “had to” on a branch, then rank the branches using the text’s own priority marker (Above all). The repeated “had to” becomes the discovery point: You ask “Why does the writer repeat ‘had to’ so many times? What does it do to the reader?” and learners find that the repetition builds the weight of responsibility.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 10’s settlement; had to for past necessity; as soon as.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reducing Adam’s life on Earth to survival: The chapter adds moral struggle and governing the Earth.
Treating the repeated “had to” as careless repetition rather than deliberate emphasis.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: No sooner had … than … (No sooner had one ended than another began.) ↔ As soon as … · repeated had to ↔ It was necessary for + person + to · Above all (priority) vs After all (reason) · X means Y for a wider consequence (the removal of Allah from the human mind means the removal of meaning and purpose from human life) · while for two groups · want someone not to ↔ not want someone to.
Notice (Activity 1): Ask “Was there any rest between the struggles? Which words make the sentence feel so fast?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the lines with Above all / means / while, then rewrite had to, the negative wish and the no-sooner sentence.
Likely errors: *No sooner one had ended · *No sooner … when · After all used for priority · *It was necessary him to work hard.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph about a person or group entering a demanding new environment (a new school, a first job, a new country).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Inversion is stressed on the contrast: “no SOONer had ONE ENDed | than aNOTHer beGAN”.
Weak “had to” /hædtə/ in a list, strong verbs: “he had to /tə/ mainTAIN, CULtivate, conSTRUCT, and POPulate the EARTH”.
Priority frame with a pause: “aBOVE ALL, | he had to STRUGgle …”.
Word focus: CON-flict (noun), dis-PLACE-ment, con-TIN-u-ous, CUL-ti-vate, POP-u-late.
beforeReading: Ask: “When you start at a new school, what do you suddenly have to do?” Pairs list four “had to” sentences, then rank them.
duringReading: Circle every “had to”.
Mark the no-sooner sentence and the “Above all” sentence.
Underline the sentence with “means” and the contrast with “while”.
Find the one thing that eased Adam’s grief.
