afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Interpret “No sooner … than …” in Activity 1, complete priority/consequence/contrast in Activity 2, rewrite necessity, negation and time in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 responsibility paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “new school” had-to list, pairs rank their four sentences; 4–12 Listen and read, then count the “had to” forms (learners call out the number and the verbs); 12–18 Responsibility web on A3 in groups: Adam in the center, each “had to” on a branch, branches colored practical / moral / social, then groups mark the branch the text ranks first (Above all); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (Any rest between the struggles?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, quick contrast of “above all” and “after all” with a school example; 31–38 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a demanding new environment, partner checks for one “no sooner … than” and two different kinds of “had to”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which responsibilities does the chapter name, and which comes “above all”?
What does the chapter say happens when Allah is removed from the human mind?
What eased Adam’s grief, and why might responsibility bring comfort?
interactiveTips: Use the Struggle on Earth hotspot with the no-sooner sentence and “Above all”.
Use the Building Human Life hotspot with the list maintain / cultivate / construct / populate.
Read the hadith at the start as source text with its reference; do not gap it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a web template with three branches labelled practical / moral / social and the frames “He had to ____.”, “Above all, ____.” and “No sooner had ____ than ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Connect practical and moral responsibility in one paragraph using “means” for a wider consequence and “while” for a contrast.

formativeAssessment: Lists responsibilities with evidence and identifies the priority.
Explains the no-sooner inversion.
Uses had to / necessary for, above all and means accurately.
expectedResponses: On Earth Adam faced one struggle after another, had to work, protect himself and, above all, struggle against the spirit of evil; he also had to maintain, cultivate, construct and populate the Earth, and governing it was the only thing that eased his grief.
content.transferTask: Write one realistic plan to take care of a shared space at school, with two “had to / must” responsibilities and one priority.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the effect of the repeated “had to”, and did they turn stewardship into a concrete action?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups, make a responsibility web on A3: Adam in the center, each “had to” on a branch. Color the branches practical, moral or social, then mark the one the text puts first.
checkQuestions: What color system do you use? (practical, moral, social)
Which branch do you mark? (the one after “Above all”)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that groups mark the struggle against the spirit of evil as the priority. During Activity 1, listen for the meaning of “no sooner … than”. In the Use task, check for two different kinds of had to.

exitTicket: Write one “No sooner had … than …” sentence and one “Above all, …” sentence about your first week at this school.

rubricLevels.secure: Lists responsibilities with evidence and names the priority.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “Above all” and ask what follows it.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells above all from after all with an example.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one school sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains no sooner … than as one event right after another.
rubricLevels.notYet: Rewrite it as “As soon as …, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a concrete transfer about a demanding new place.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the new-school list from the hook as material.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam's responsibilities on earth include work, morals and caring for others, 'above all' remembering Allah. Every culture ranks its priorities.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: If an English-speaking exchange student asked 'What matters most in a Turkish family?', what would you answer? What do you think they might answer about theirs?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Avoid stereotypes such as 'Western families are cold' or 'Eastern families are crowded'. Learners give one fact they know and mark guesses as guesses.

content.chapter: Chapter 12: The Conflict of Habil and Qabil
objectives: Explain why Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted, according to the chapter, without linking acceptance to occupation.
Compare the story’s narration with the verse (Ma’idah: 27), which does not give the brothers’ names.
Discover why the chapter uses the passive to focus on the outcome, how “while” sets two actions side by side, and how the writer marks the limits of the account.
Separate sincerity of intention from role or status.
content.pedagogy: Use a three-layer table: Story narration / quoted verse / the writer’s comments on the source. Learners notice that the names Habil and Qabil come from the narration, not from the verse. The language work begins from the key outcome sentence: You ask “Why does the sentence begin with ‘Qabil’s sacrifice’? Is the doer hidden?” and learners discover that this passive is about focus, not about an unknown agent.
priorKnowledge: Passive voice; while for contrast; according to from earlier chapters.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Assuming farming or herding decided the outcome: The text gives “his insincerity in his offering” as the reason.
Claiming the Qur’anic verse names the brothers: The chapter says they “are referred to as Adam (pbuh)’s two sons without their names being given”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive for outcome focus with the agent stated (Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah because of his insincerity in his offering.) · while ↔ on the other hand / by contrast (Habil offered his best cattle while Qabil offered his worst grain.) · passive -ing after a preposition (without their names being given) ↔ active (without giving their names) · source limits (without mentioning names / It does not openly mention … / according to the Qur’an, … / Although we don’t know the whole story).
Notice (Activity 1): Ask “Why does the writer begin with ‘Qabil’s sacrifice’? Is the doer hidden? What comes after ‘because of’?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the while-sentence as two sentences and the passive -ing as an active, then match each source-limiting expression with its signal.
Likely errors: *because of he was insincere · *without their names being gave · the belief that a passive always hides the doer.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence source-aware contrast paragraph about a non-story dispute or report.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress across while: “HAbil offered his BEST CATtle | while QAbil offered his WORST GRAIN”.
Passive negative: “was NOT acCEPTed by alLAH | because of his inSINcerity”.
Source frames as chunks: “acCORDing to the QurAN, |”, “ALthough we DON’T KNOW the WHOLE STORy, |”.
Word focus: SAC-ri-fice, in-sin-CER-i-ty, PI-ous (/ˈpaɪəs/), HAR-mo-ny, OF-fer-ing.
beforeReading: Ask: “Two students hand in projects. One is careful, one is rushed. What tells the teacher more: which subject each student likes, or how each project was made?” Collect answers without judging any subject.
duringReading: Mark the two roles (cultivated the land / raised cattle) and the two offerings.
Underline the reason the sacrifice was not accepted.
Box the quoted verse and note that it gives no names.
Circle the four source-limiting expressions in the last paragraph.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with an offering / intention / evidence table.
Language Focus: Explain the passive in Activity 1, rewrite contrast and omission in Activity 2, match the source limits in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 source-aware contrast paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: careful vs rushed project, what tells the teacher more?; 4–12 Listen and read, then mark roles, offerings and the reason; 12–19 Three-layer table in pairs: narration / verse / writer’s comments on the source, learners check where the names appear and where they do not, one pair presents; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (Is the doer hidden?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners say which expression admits a gap; 31–38 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a dispute or report from the news or school life, with one passive for the outcome and one source limit, partner checks that the conclusion stays inside the evidence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is occupation not the reason for acceptance?
Why does the Qur’an, according to the chapter, not give the names or other details?
How does “Although we don’t know the whole story” make the writer more trustworthy?
interactiveTips: Use The Two Offerings hotspot with the while-sentence and the outcome sentence.
Use the From Conflict to Threat hotspot calmly with Qabil’s anger, without role-play.
Keep the story’s names separate from the quoted verse.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give columns role / offering / outcome / reason / source status and the frame “____ was not accepted because of ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph with two levels of certainty (what the source says / what we do not know) and justify each.

formativeAssessment: Gives the text’s reason for the outcome.
Explains the purpose of the passive.
Identifies the source limits accurately.
expectedResponses: Habil offered his best cattle while Qabil offered his worst grain; Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted because of his insincerity, and the chapter notes that the Qur’an tells the story without names because only its wisdom needs to be known.
content.transferTask: Analyse a case where the quality of effort says more than role or status, and state one thing the evidence cannot tell you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover that the passive here is about focus, and did they keep narration, verse and the writer’s comments distinct?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, complete the three-layer table: narration, verse and the writer’s comments on the source. Check where the names of the brothers appear and where they do not.
checkQuestions: How many layers? (three)
What do you check about the names? (where they appear)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs notice that the verse gives no names. Listen during Activity 1 for learners who say why the doer is hidden. In the Use task, check that the conclusion stays inside the evidence.

exitTicket: Write one passive sentence that focuses on an outcome and one sentence that admits what we do not know.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the text’s reason for the outcome: insincerity.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the word “because” in the sentence about the offering.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the passive “was not accepted”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who accepted? Why is that not said?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names what the source does not tell us.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “The Qur’an does not tell us …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the conclusion in proportion to the evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does the evidence really show this much?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The verse does not name the brothers; the names Habil and Qabil come from tradition. In English the same brothers are usually called Cain and Abel.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Why does the same story have different names in Turkish, Arabic and English? What other names change across languages (Süleyman / Solomon, Davud / David)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice shared stories between traditions without claiming the accounts are identical. They keep each detail attributed to its source.

content.chapter: Chapter 13: Habil’s Response & Human Moral Capacity
objectives: Explain Habil’s refusal to use violence as a choice, not as weakness.
Explain the chapter’s view that humans “have the potential for both good and evil” and where it locates “the path to goodness”.
Discover how the writer concedes a point and then stresses another (although, At first glance … may seem …, However, it is important to remember …), and the forms of Habil’s advice and condition.
Discuss self-control and compassion in low-stakes, non-violent situations.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds two portraits from the adjectives in the text (Habil: intelligent, respectful … / his brother: arrogant, selfish …) and a map of Habil’s speech: diagnosis → advice → condition → consequence. The theme is handled calmly; no threats are acted out. Lesson 2 asks how the writer argues: Learners sort pairs of sentences and discover that the first part is conceded and the second is stressed, then practise Habil’s advice and condition forms.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 12’s threat; although and however; if-clauses.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reading “At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable. However, …” as an excuse for Qabil: The chapter goes on to call him arrogant, sinful and responsible for “the consequence of your sin”.
Thinking that the potential for evil makes self-control impossible: The text says “The path to goodness is in controlling evil thoughts and actions”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: concession + main point (although Qabil had the intention to kill, Habil did not adopt an aggressive attitude / At first glance, … may seem unacceptable. However, it is important to remember …) · Although X, Y ↔ X. However / Nevertheless, Y · participle of purpose (Hoping to lessen the hatred in his brother, …) · advice (It is better that you repent to Allah and forget …) · real condition (But if you do not, then I will …) · did not + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort three pairs into “accepted or mentioned first” and “the point the writer stresses”. Ask: “In each pair, which part does the writer want you to remember? What happens to the first part?”
Build (Activities 2–3): split the concession into two sentences and expand “Hoping to …”, then correct *repented, *if you will not and *did not wanted.
Likely errors: *Although …, but … · *It is better that you repented · *if you will not, … · *did not wanted.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph about a measured response to a non-story conflict (a group-work dispute, an online argument).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Concession clause rises, main clause falls: “alTHOUGH QAbil had the inTENtion to KILL↗, | HAbil did NOT adopt an agGRESsive ATtitude↘”.
Read the verse slowly and calmly: “EVen if you RAISE your HAND against me | … I will NOT RAISE my HAND …”.
Advice with stress on the verb: “It is BETter that you rePENT …”.
Word focus: ag-GRES-sive, po-TEN-tial, MOD-er-ate (adjective), dis-o-BE-di-ent, com-PAS-sion, re-BEL-lious.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does strength look like when someone is angry with you? Is walking away weak or strong?” Collect ideas, keeping examples harmless.
duringReading: Mark the verse and what it shows about Habil.
List the adjectives for each brother.
Underline “although”, “At first glance … may seem” and “However, it is important to remember”.
Map Habil’s speech: diagnosis, advice, condition, consequence.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge with claim–evidence–explanation and leave a bridge note.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on concession, purpose, advice and condition (Activities 1–3).
Write or say the Activity 4 conflict-response paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: Is walking away weak or strong? quick think-pair-share; 5–14 Listen and read, then reread the verse and the last speech; 14–23 Two portraits in pairs: Adjectives for Habil / for his brother, each with the sentence, then one sentence explaining the contrast with “This contrasted sharply with …”; 23–31 Speech map in groups of three: Diagnosis (you are turning away …) → advice (It is better that …) → condition (if you do not …) → consequence (You alone will bear …), groups compare maps; 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note: One sentence on why Habil’s choice was strength; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the speech map; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as discovery (which part does the writer want you to remember?), learners state the rule for concession; 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then a quick oral round: Learners concede and stress with a school topic (Although homework takes time, …); 22–33 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a harmless conflict, with a concession, a “may / can”, a purpose, a piece of advice and an if-clause; 33–38 Pairs read and name the stressed point in each other’s concession; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the chapter present Habil’s refusal as moral strength?
How does “At first glance … may seem” prepare a wider view without excusing Qabil?
Where does the chapter locate “the path to goodness”?
interactiveTips: Use the Habil Refuses Violence hotspot with the verse and the “although” sentence.
Use the Human Moral Capacity hotspot with “both good and evil” and “The path to goodness …”.
Keep all transfer situations low-stakes and non-violent; never role-play the threat.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give frames: “Although ____, ____.”, “At first glance, ____ may seem ____. However, ____.”, “It is better that you ____.”, “If you do not ____, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Compare two possible responses to the same harmless conflict and use modal language to qualify the likely result of each.

formativeAssessment: Explains Habil’s choice with evidence.
Identifies the conceded and the stressed point.
Uses advice and real-condition forms accurately.
expectedResponses: Although Qabil intended to kill, Habil did not become aggressive; the chapter admits that people can be jealous or harmful but says the path to goodness is controlling evil thoughts and actions, and Habil advises his brother to repent, warning that he alone will bear the consequence.
content.transferTask: Write two measured responses to a low-stakes conflict and explain the likely consequence of each.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see that the concession does not excuse Qabil, and did they discover the concede-then-stress pattern before I named it?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, write adjectives for both brothers with a sentence for each. Then, in groups of three, build the speech map: diagnosis, advice, condition and consequence.
checkQuestions: How many parts does the speech map have? (four)
What do you add to each adjective? (a sentence from the text)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen in the think-pair-share for the idea that walking away can be strength. In Lesson 2, check the oral round: the stressed point should come after the comma. In the Use task, check for advice and a real if-clause.

exitTicket: Write one “Although …, …” sentence about a disagreement and one piece of advice with “It is better that you …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Habil refuses to use violence. Non-violence as moral strength appears in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which figures from different cultures are remembered for refusing violence (Habil in this story, Mahatma Gandhi in India, Martin Luther King Jr. in the USA)? What did each refuse, and why?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Keep each figure in their own context. Learners compare the choice, not the beliefs or the countries.

objectives: Trace, calmly and without graphic detail, how restraints failed and how the consequences accumulated for Qabil.
Explain why the chapter says Allah sent the two ravens (“As a mercy, and to show that human dignity had to be preserved even after death”).
Discover how verb forms show a state already reached versus a process going on, how “nor” adds a second negative with inversion, and how the passive keeps a result or a lost restraint in focus.
Connect the chapter with human dignity and learning from an example.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 is a consequence map, not a retelling of violence: The teacher reads the first paragraph once, calmly, and learners note only the failed restraints (the brother’s request, fear of Allah’s punishment, family considerations). Then they trace the aftermath: Adam’s search and grief, Qabil’s burden, the ravens. Lesson 2 asks how the verb forms make the burden grow: learners sort state vs process and discover the inversion after “nor”.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 13’s speech; past perfect; passive; reported speech.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating the raven episode as a random detail: The chapter gives its purpose (mercy and human dignity).
Assuming the passive (“Even familial considerations were given up”) removes Qabil’s responsibility: The surrounding sentences keep him as the actor.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: state already reached (His anger had now lessened / his heart was burdened with guilt) vs process going on or beginning (He was getting tired … / wandering from place to place trying to hide it / It also started to have a stench) · nor + auxiliary + subject (This brotherly request did nothing to lessen the hatred in Qabil’s heart, nor did he show fear of Allah’s punishment.) · passive be + past participle (Even familial considerations were given up / human dignity had to be preserved) · backshift after a past reporting verb (replied that he was not his brother’s keeper).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five parts into “a state already reached” and “something going on or just beginning”. Ask: “Which forms tell you something is finished, and which show it still growing?”
Build (Activities 2–3): rebuild the nor-sentence from chunks, then correct *were gave up, *had to preserve and *replied that he is not.
Likely errors: *nor he showed fear · *were gave up · *had to preserve (active: dignity does not preserve anything) · *replied that he is not.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence consequence-and-realisation paragraph about a harmless situation (ignoring warnings about a deadline, hiding a broken object).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Inversion after nor, stress on the auxiliary: “… NOR DID he SHOW FEAR of alLAH’s PUNishment”.
Developing state: “he was GETting TIRED | under the BURden of the CORPSE”.
-ed endings: lessened /d/, burdened /d/, carried /d/, started /ɪd/, preserved /d/, rolled /d/, covered /d/.
Word focus: fa-MIL-ial, CRIM-i-nal, CORPSE (/kɔːps/, not “corps”), GUILT (silent u), vic-TO-ri-ous. Keep a calm, even voice throughout.
beforeReading: Ask: “What usually stops people from doing something seriously wrong?” Pairs list three kinds of restraint (conscience, family, fear of consequences). Keep the list for the reading.
duringReading: Teacher reads the first paragraph once, calmly: Learners tick which restraints from their list failed.
Mark Adam’s search and his grief.
Underline the state and process forms in the Qabil paragraph.
Box the purpose given for the ravens.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the sequencing Quick Challenge and write a bridge note: One failed restraint and one purpose of the raven episode.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on state vs process, nor + inversion and passive/reported forms (Activities 1–3).
Write or say the Activity 4 consequence-and-realisation paragraph about a harmless situation.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Hook: What stops people from doing wrong? pairs list three restraints; 5–10 Teacher reads the first paragraph once, calmly, learners tick the failed restraints on their list; 10–17 Listen to the rest and read along; 17–27 Consequence map in pairs: Failed restraints → the act (named in one word only) → Adam’s grief → Qabil’s growing burden → the ravens → purpose (mercy, dignity), each link with a short quoted phrase; 27–32 Whole-class discussion: Why does the chapter give a purpose for the ravens?; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the map without books; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as discovery (finished or still growing?), learners label the forms; 12–20 Activity 2 sentence-building, then learners make one “nor did …” sentence about a harmless school event, Activity 3 in pairs; 20–32 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph (for example a student ignores two reminders about a project, stress grows, a classmate’s example shows a better way); 32–37 Peer check: Find the nor-sentence, the passive and the “was getting” form; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which restraints failed, according to the first paragraph?
How does the text show Qabil’s burden growing?
Why does the chapter give a purpose for the raven episode?
interactiveTips: Use The Crime and Its Consequence hotspot only for the consequence map, not for detail about the act.
Use The Two Ravens hotspot with the purpose sentence (“to show that human dignity had to be preserved”).
Never role-play or draw the violence; keep discussion on dignity, consequence and learning.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give boxes failed restraint / result / growing burden / lesson and the frames “____ did nothing to ____, nor did ____.” and “He was getting ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Explain in a short paragraph how the passive “were given up” changes the focus without removing responsibility.

formativeAssessment: Maps consequences without graphic detail.
Distinguishes state and process forms.
Uses nor + inversion and the passive accurately.
expectedResponses: Neither his brother’s request nor fear of punishment stopped Qabil; afterwards his anger lessened, guilt burdened him and he grew tired carrying the body, until Allah, as a mercy and to show that human dignity must be preserved, sent two ravens and one buried the other.
content.transferTask: Map a harmless poor decision, its accumulating consequences and a later moment of learning from an example.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners analyse consequence and dignity without sensationalising the act, and did the state/process sort make the growing burden visible?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: Listen calmly as I read the first paragraph and tick the restraints that failed. Then, in pairs, build the consequence map with a short quoted phrase on each link. Name the act in one word only.
checkQuestions: How many words do you use for the act? (one)
Do we act out or draw this chapter? (no)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the reading calm and stop any graphic retelling. Check that maps end with the purpose of the ravens: mercy and dignity. In Lesson 2, listen for the nor sentence about a harmless school event.

exitTicket: Write one “nor did …” sentence about a harmless situation and explain the raven episode in one calm analytical sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Maps the consequences without graphic detail.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the map links as headings to fill.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells a finished state from a growing process (was getting).
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is it finished, or still growing?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses nor with inversion and the passive accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the model “Neither … nor … stopped him”.

rubricLevels.secure: Discusses the chapter with care and respect.
rubricLevels.notYet: Remind the class of the calm reading rule.

interculturalFocus.notice: Allah sends the ravens 'to show that human dignity had to be preserved even after death'. Respect for the dead is a value across cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask a general question only: Which values about the dead are shared in many cultures (burial with care, remembering, not speaking ill of the dead)? Is there an English saying about this?
interculturalFocus.perspective: This is a sensitive chapter. Do not ask about personal loss or specific funeral rituals; keep to shared values.

objectives: Separate what happened (the raven, Qabil’s regret, the first burial, Adam’s grief) from the writer’s interpretation of it.
Explain the writer’s interpretation: The consequence of choosing evil, rooted in jealousy.
Discover the purpose + embedded how-clause, compact clauses (participle, reduced passive, non-defining which) and the wh-cleft that announces interpretation.
Explain how Adam (pbuh) responded to loss with prayer and work.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has a clear hinge: “What is essentially being described here is …”. Learners draw a line in the text at that sentence and label everything before it “event” and everything after it “interpretation” (except the last lines about Adam, which return to events). The discovery question is: “How does the writer tell you he is stepping back from the story?” Learners then unpack the chapter’s compact clauses into full ones.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 14’s ravens; relative clauses; event vs interpretation from earlier chapters.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Treating the interpretive sentences (“It arises from jealousy …”, “Qabil represents …”) as part of the quoted verse.
Equating Qabil’s regret with completed repair or with the repentance of Adam in Chapter 9.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: purpose + embedded how-clause (to show him how he might cover the corpse of his brother) · participle clause (Witnessing this, Qabil was overcome with shame and guilt.) · reduced passive relative (the type of person dominated by evil) · non-defining which (jealousy, which defeats the feelings of love and compassion of brotherhood) · wh-cleft as an interpretive frame (What is essentially being described here is the consequence of choosing evil.) · while for a character contrast.
Notice (Activity 1): Ask “Is ‘how he might cover the corpse of his brother’ a question? What did Qabil not yet know?” Learners notice statement word order after “how”.
Build (Activities 2–3): expand “Witnessing this”, “dominated by evil” and the which-clause into full clauses, then sort “what happened” and “the writer’s interpretation”.
Likely errors: *how might he cover (question order) · *a person dominating by evil · *It arises from jealousy which it defeats … · reading interpretation as narrated fact.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence event-to-interpretation paragraph about a non-story situation, with the frame “What is essentially described here is …” (the app’s frame; the story itself says “What is essentially being described here is …”, and both are correct).
content.pronunciationFocus:
The wh-cleft has two halves with a pause: “WHAT is ESsentially being deSCRIBED here | is the CONsequence of CHOOSing EVil”.
Participle clause as its own chunk: “WITnessing THIS, | QAbil was overCOME with SHAME and GUILT”.
Contrast with while: “QAbil repreSENTS … | while HAbil repreSENTS the RIGHTeous PERson …”.
Word focus: FALSE-hood, CON-se-quence, JEAL-ous-y, RIGHT-eous (/ˈraɪtʃəs/), IL-lus-trat-ing.
beforeReading: Tell a two-sentence neutral story (“A student left the lab untidy. The next group lost ten minutes cleaning.”), then add “What this really shows is …”. Ask: “Which sentence changed from telling to interpreting? Which words told you?”
duringReading: Box the quoted verse (Ma’idah: 31).
Draw a line at “What is essentially being described here …”.
Label sentences event or interpretation.
Underline what Adam did after his loss.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using event evidence.
Language Focus: Analyse the purpose and how-clause in Activity 1, expand the compact clauses in Activity 2, sort event vs interpretation in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 event-to-interpretation paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: The untidy-lab story, learners find the sentence where interpretation begins; 4–12 Listen and read, then box the verse; 12–18 Hinge line: Pairs draw the line at the wh-cleft and label each sentence event / interpretation, then compare with another pair and resolve disagreements with the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (Is it a question?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, learners explain why the compact version links cause and effect more tightly; 31–38 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a school or community event, events first, then the cleft, then the interpretation, partner marks where the interpretation begins; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which exact words announce the move from event to interpretation?
Why does the chapter trace the consequence back to jealousy?
How does Adam respond to losing both sons, and what does that show about responsibility?
interactiveTips: Use the Qabil’s Regret hotspot with the verse and “Witnessing this …”.
Use the Adam’s Continued Responsibility hotspot with the last sentence (“because he had to work hard for his daily bread”).
Quote the story verbatim (“What is essentially being described here …”) and accept both the story version and the app frame in learners’ writing.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give labels event / purpose / interpretation / contrast and the frames “What is essentially described here is ____.” and “____ represents ____, while ____ represents ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two interpretations of the same harmless event and justify which is better supported by the facts they gave.

formativeAssessment: Separates events from interpretation correctly.
Explains the embedded how-clause.
Expands compact clauses accurately.
expectedResponses: The raven showed Qabil how to cover his brother’s body; Qabil was filled with shame and regret and buried his brother, the first burial; the writer then interprets this as the consequence of choosing evil, arising from jealousy, and contrasts Qabil with Habil, while Adam prayed and returned to work.
content.transferTask: Describe a harmless event, then mark and justify the sentence where interpretation begins.
content.teacherReflection: Did the hinge line make the move from event to interpretation visible, and did learners keep regret distinct from completed repair?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw a line where the wh-cleft begins. Label every sentence event or interpretation. Then compare with another pair and settle disagreements with the text.
checkQuestions: Where do you draw the line? (at the wh-cleft)
How do you settle a disagreement? (with the text)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs keep the first burial as an event and the consequence of choosing evil as interpretation. Listen in Activity 1 for “not a question”. In the Use task, check that partners can point to where interpretation starts.

exitTicket: Write the chapter’s interpretive frame from memory and one event sentence that comes before it.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates events from interpretation correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask for each sentence “Can we see this happen?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the embedded how-clause.
rubricLevels.notYet: Rewrite the clause as a full sentence together.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses an interpretive frame such as “What this shows is …”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame to complete.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives an interpretation that the events support.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Which event shows this?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Qabil's regret is traced back to jealousy. Jealousy is described in proverbs of many languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Compare a Turkish proverb about envy (Haset eden kendini yer) with an English one (Jealousy is the green-eyed monster, from Shakespeare's Othello). What image does each culture use?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Colours and images for feelings change across languages: green in English, yellow or black in other languages. Learners collect one image from each language they know.

objectives: Describe Adam’s prophetic role as continuing actions (advising, telling, calling, warning).
Keep the detail about Seth at its source level (“It was narrated that …”).
Discover parallel -ing actions, by + -ing, tempt + person + to, and how reported “would” becomes “will” in direct speech.
Explain Adam’s legacy: Prophets with “different names and miracles” but “united in one thing”.
content.pedagogy: Learners build a legacy chain: Role (a prophet advising, telling, calling) → warning (his own experience, Qabil) → succession (Seth, reported) → message (prophets will come) → peace at death. The language grows from the two key sentences: Learners notice that the three -ing actions are one role, and that “would” in “told his children that Allah would not leave man alone” is Adam’s own “will” seen from the past.
priorKnowledge: Reported speech; would from Chapter 10; It is reported that.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Reading succession as political power: The chapter describes teaching (the hours of the day and night with their acts of worship).
Treating “It was narrated that …” as either false or as the writer’s own direct claim.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: impersonal reporting frame (It was narrated that when Adam (pbuh)’s death drew near, he appointed his son Seth …) · parallel -ing actions (a prophet advising …, telling … and calling …) · by + -ing (warned them by telling them …) · tempt + person + to-infinitive (how Satan had tempted Qabil to kill his brother) · reported would ↔ direct will (told his children that Allah would not leave man alone …) · different …, but united in … .
Notice (Activity 1): true/false. Ask: “Does ‘It was narrated that’ say the report is false? Then what does it tell us?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct *to call, *by tell and *tempted Qabil killing, then turn Adam’s reported words into direct speech (will not leave / will be united).
Likely errors: *and to call them (broken parallel list) · *by tell · *tempted Qabil killing · keeping “would” in direct speech.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence legacy paragraph about a person or institution passing guidance to a later generation.
content.pronunciationFocus:
A list of three parallel actions rises, rises, falls: “adVISing his CHILdren↗, | TELLing them about alLAH↗, | and CALLing them to beLIEVE in HIM↘”.
Contrast and unity: “DIFFerent NAMES and MIRacles, | but … uNIted in ONE thing”.
Numbers: “one hundred and four scrolls”, “fifty were sent down to Seth”.
Word focus: suc-CES-sor, LEG-a-cy, MIR-a-cles, ap-POINT-ed, ap-PRO-pri-ate.
beforeReading: Ask: “When a teacher who has taught at a school for many years retires, what should she pass on, and to whom?” Learners list two things (knowledge, a warning, a routine).
duringReading: Underline the three -ing actions of the prophet.
Mark the warning and what it was based on.
Box “It was narrated that …” and the detail it qualifies.
Mark Adam’s message about the prophets.
afterReading: Complete the four-pair matching Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Judge the reporting frame in Activity 1, correct the verb patterns in Activity 2, turn reported into direct speech in Activity 3.
Write or say the Activity 4 legacy paragraph.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: What should a retiring teacher pass on? pairs list two things; 4–12 Listen and read, then underline the -ing actions and box the reporting frame; 12–18 Legacy chain in pairs: Five links (role, warning, succession, message, peace at the end) each with a quoted phrase, pairs mark which link is reported and which is narrated directly; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery (false, or passed on by others?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 as a short role-shift: One learner reads the reported sentence, the partner says it as direct speech; 31–38 Use: The Activity 4 paragraph about a person or institution that passes on guidance (a grandparent, a sports club, a school founder), with “It is said that …” or “According to …”, partner checks the -ing list is parallel; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How do repeated actions make Adam’s prophetic role active?
Why is the Seth detail introduced with “It was narrated that”?
How can prophets have “different names and miracles” and still be “united in one thing”?
interactiveTips: Use the Seth’s Successorship hotspot with the reported sentence and keep its source frame visible.
Use the Adam’s Legacy hotspot with the message about the prophets.
Read the hadith about the scrolls as quoted source text; do not gap it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give boxes role / warning / successor / message and the frames “He was ____, ____-ing, ____-ing and ____-ing.” and “They are different in ____, but united in ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Link each element of Adam’s legacy to an earlier chapter of the book (for example the warning to Chapter 7, the message to Chapter 9).

formativeAssessment: Describes the role through parallel actions.
Keeps the reported detail at its source level.
Converts reported would to direct will accurately.
expectedResponses: Adam advised, taught and warned his children from his own experience; it was narrated that he appointed Seth as his successor; before his death he told them that Allah would send prophets with different names and miracles, united in the call to Allah’s straight path, and when he recognized the Angel of Death his heart filled with peace.
content.transferTask: Write what useful knowledge and one warning you would pass on to a younger learner, and why.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read legacy as active transmission, and did they keep the reported detail about Seth at its source level?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, build the legacy chain with five links. Add a quoted phrase to each. Mark which link is reported and which is told directly.
checkQuestions: How many links? (five)
What do you mark? (reported or told directly)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “it was narrated that” marks the succession of Seth as reported. During the role-shift, listen for would becoming will. In the Use task, check that the -ing list is parallel.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with three parallel -ing actions and turn “He said that the prophets would come.” into direct speech.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes Adam’s role through parallel actions with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the three -ing verbs in the first sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the reported detail at its source level.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does the writer say it directly, or report it?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses a parallel -ing list and the right verb patterns.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give a list with one wrong form to fix.

rubricLevels.secure: Changes reported would into direct will correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Model one change, then let the learner do the next.

interculturalFocus.notice: Seth continues Adam's message, and the chapter says prophets had 'different names and miracles' but one message. The same figures often carry different names across languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English names correspond to Şit, Nuh and İdris (Seth, Noah, Enoch)? How would you explain to an English reader that these are the same figures?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners use 'known in English as …' to bridge names without claiming that every tradition tells the story the same way.

content.chapter: Chapter 17: The Challenge of Satan & Human Value
objectives: Explain how the verses limit Satan’s claim (“I will mislead them all”) with exceptions.
Explain the chapter’s view that Satan only looks strong because of human weakness, lack of morals and carelessness.
Discover how the chapter narrows broad claims (except for), focuses on the real cause (it-cleft / wh-cleft), and concedes one point while stressing another (not so much … but rather …).
Synthesise the book’s answer to “Where should man truly find his sense of value?” with evidence from several chapters.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 works on scope: Learners mark every universal word (all, no authority) and the exception that follows, then build a “real power vs apparent power” T-chart from the it-cleft. Lesson 2 is the synthesis lesson: After the Language Focus, learners collect evidence from early, middle and late chapters to answer the book’s final question, and they end with a genuine open question of their own. Earlier-chapter evidence comes before personal reflection.
priorKnowledge: All chapters; concession and although; source qualification.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Presenting Satan as having unlimited power: The verses say “Over My servants you have no authority, except for the sinners who follow you”.
Reading “does not focus so much on Satan’s anti-God position” as a denial of his rebellion: The bracket says he “is unquestionably a rebel against Allah”.
Returning to origin as the basis of human value, which the book rejected in Chapters 2 and 5.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: broad claim narrowed by an exception (I will mislead them all. / Except for Your sincere servants among them. / Over My servants you have no authority, except for the sinners who follow you.) · it-cleft ↔ wh-cleft for the real cause (it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and carefulness that make Satan look so strong ↔ What makes Satan look so strong is …) · Learning about Adam (pbuh)’s tale is to know … ↔ By learning …, we come to know … · concession in brackets + not so much … but rather … · In fact.
Notice (Activity 1): matching. Ask: “Is ‘them all’ really all? Who narrows the claim the first time, and who the second time?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the it-cleft as a wh-cleft and “Learning … is to know …” with By learning …, then choose the summary that keeps what is conceded and what is stressed.
Likely errors: *it is only man’s weakness what makes · *What makes Satan look so strong are … · *except of · turning “not so much … but rather” into a denial.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence qualified argument about an influence that seems powerful but depends on human choices (for example a social-media trend, peer pressure), ending with a genuine open question.
content.pronunciationFocus:
The exception is its own tone group: “and I will misLEAD them ALL. | exCEPT for Your SINcere SERvants …”.
Focus stress in the cleft: “it is ONly MAN’s WEAKness … | that make SAtan LOOK so STRONG”.
Concession in brackets on a lower, quicker pitch; the main clause returns to normal pitch.
Word focus: au-THOR-i-ty, mis-LEAD, de-SCEND-ants, per-SON-i-fies, de-TER-rent.
beforeReading: Ask learners to predict the book’s final answer to “Where does human value come from?” using evidence from at least two earlier chapters (for example Chapter 2: same soil, Chapter 3: knowledge).
duringReading: Circle every universal word (all, no) and underline the exception that follows.
Mark the concession in brackets and the “but rather” that follows it.
Underline the it-cleft about Satan’s apparent strength.
Box the final question.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the final Quick Challenge with three pieces of evidence.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on exception, clefts and concession (Activities 1–3), then the Activity 4 qualified argument ending in an open question.
Then continue through the book-ending sequence in this order: Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Retrieval: Pairs predict the book’s answer about human value with two earlier chapters; 5–14 Listen and read, then read the verses again in meaning groups; 14–22 Scope hunt in pairs: Every universal word and its exception, two pairs present; 22–30 Real vs apparent power T-chart from the it-cleft, learners add what the chapter says makes Satan “look so strong”; 30–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note: One claim about human value with one piece of evidence; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the T-chart; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as discovery (Is “them all” really all?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 12–20 Evidence gallery: Groups of four collect one quotation each from early, middle and late chapters on A3 sheets, then walk and read two other groups’ sheets; 20–32 Use: The Activity 4 argument about an influence that depends on human choices, ending with a genuine open question; 32–37 Pairs read and judge whether the question follows from the argument; 37–40 Exit ticket and preview of the post-book sequence.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide — Prophet Adam (B2)
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned B2 guide with evidence-based reading, inductive grammar as discourse and realistic 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 17 chapter units: Chapters 1–3, 5–6, 8–9, 11–12 and 15–16 are planned for 40 minutes; Chapters 4, 7, 10, 13, 14 and 17 are planned as 40 + 40 minutes. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: Upper-secondary learners studying English at approximately CEFR B2.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended narrative and explanation, distinguish evidence from interpretation, qualify source-based claims, and produce connected analytical spoken and written responses.
metadata.purpose: Develop B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh): evidence-based comprehension, source-aware interpretation, the chapter-specific Language Focus and connected analytical production about the learners’ own world, without adding facts outside the book.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks the key idea. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does in the argument (the rule is confirmed only after they have formulated it), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about a new, non-story situation. At B2 the emphasis is on stance, qualification, evidence versus interpretation and source boundaries. Denser chapters are divided into two 40-minute lessons rather than compressed. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 17 Quick Challenges, evidence and source checks, chapter Language Focus tasks and B2 production, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Language Review, Vocabulary Challenge, Master Glossary review and Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs with one short, chapter-specific question, card task, image or prediction, and keep the predictions open until the text confirms them.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then reread for the chapter’s own evidence structure: source, stance strength, cause chain, contrast, concession, sequence, voice, exception or the move from event to interpretation. Do not interrupt the first reading to teach every word.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 response about a new situation. In 40 + 40 chapters, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter Word Notes and the analytical words needed for the chapter’s key relationship (source, stance, cause, concession, exception).
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, quotation, image or discourse relation before any definition is given.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse Word Notes in Language Focus production, discussion, exit tickets, the Vocabulary Challenge and the Master Glossary.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based, taught as discourse. Start from the story sentence, ask one or two meaning questions (What does this form do here? How sure is the writer? Whose view is this?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: source-grounding (We learn … from, Based on); passive for topic focus (is told, is portrayed as); not … but … / rather than
Ch2: non-defining vs defining relative clause (from which / which is …); passive for topic focus; As an example / So, in essence / did not …, but …
Ch3: stance strength (shows, means, refer to / points to / could be); had to be + past participle; reduced passive after a noun (the names taught to)
Ch4: not alternatives …, but rather …; require + person + to-infinitive; necessary / essential for … to …; However, which, through, both vs either
Ch5: clarification (which is, in other words, that is); because / since; On the other hand; X, yet Y ↔ Although X, Y; because ↔ therefore
Ch6: imperatives that permit, command and forbid; for fear that; while = whereas; by + -ing ↔ because / when + clause; will for firm intention
Ch7: present simple for a general truth in a past narrative; participle clause; As soon as + past perfect ↔ No sooner had … than; if + present; might; had warned
Ch8: negative question as a reminder; No, …, but …; When → so → because; source marking (is not described, It is only mentioned that, According to …, that is)
Ch9: unless = if … not; was the reason for ↔ because of; passive ↔ active; past perfect; neither … nor; must + base verb
Ch10: named vs impersonal sources (X said, It is reported that, It is said to have …); would as future in the past; was meant to; did not + base verb …, but rather …
Ch11: No sooner had … than … ↔ As soon as; had to ↔ It was necessary for … to; Above all vs After all; X means Y; while; want … not to ↔ not want … to
Ch12: passive for outcome focus with the agent stated; while ↔ on the other hand / by contrast; without their names being given ↔ without giving; source limits
Ch13: concession (although, At first glance … may seem …, However, …); Although ↔ However / Nevertheless; participle of purpose; It is better that you + base verb; if + present
Ch14: state reached vs process going on (had lessened, was burdened / was getting, started to); nor + inversion; passive (were given up, had to be preserved); reported backshift
Ch15: purpose + embedded how-clause; participle clause; reduced passive relative; non-defining which; wh-cleft interpretive frame; event vs interpretation
Ch16: It was narrated that …; parallel -ing actions; by + -ing; tempt + person + to; reported would ↔ direct will; different …, but united in …
Ch17: broad claim narrowed by except for; it-cleft ↔ wh-cleft for the real cause; Learning … is to know ↔ By learning …; not so much … but rather … with a bracketed concession

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify explicit and implicit relationships, distinguish evidence from interpretation, compare source status, infer with qualification and synthesise across chapters.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow extended narration and explanation for sequence, emphasis, stance, contrast, qualification and key evidence.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: present connected claim–evidence–explanation responses, qualify interpretations and take part in respectful analytical discussion.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce coherent B2 paragraphs using source-aware attribution, logical relationships, qualification and chapter-derived language.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — reject superiority based on origin, color or group and discuss difference respectfully.
D16 Responsibility — connect knowledge, vicegerency, repair and daily action with responsibility.
D6 Honesty — admit error, preserve source boundaries and state only what evidence supports.
D10 Humility — contrast humility, learning and repentance with arrogance.
D5 Sensitivity — notice consequences, human dignity and the feelings of others.
D20 Helpfulness — connect guidance, care and the passing on of useful knowledge with action.
D12 Patience — analyse self-control and a measured response under pressure.
D9 Compassion — examine compassion, non-harm and dignity without graphic elaboration.
languageFocus: Every one of the 17 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does in the argument before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
Preserve source attribution and certainty whenever the chapter separates quotation, report, interpretation or an unspecified detail.
At B2 the last step is always connected production about a new, non-story situation, not a retelling of the chapter.
After Chapter 17, continue in this order: Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, sentence frames, source labels, color-coded discourse relations, audio replay and oral rehearsal. Extend through source qualification, cross-chapter synthesis and independent transfer, never through extra factual content.
metadata.rubricTitle: Adam B2 Evidence, Discourse & Communication Rubric

rubricRows.excellent: Uses precise evidence and preserves source/claim boundaries.
rubricRows.good: Uses relevant evidence with minor imprecision.
rubricRows.developing: Relies on retelling, unsupported claims or blurred source status.

rubricRows.excellent: Explains cause, stance, contrast, qualification or consequence and connects ideas coherently.
rubricRows.good: Explains the main relationship with some development.
rubricRows.developing: Mostly lists events or opinions without analysing relationships.

rubricRows.excellent: Reuses chapter Language Focus accurately in a new connected context.
rubricRows.good: Uses several target patterns with understandable minor errors.
rubricRows.developing: Produces isolated examples without coherent transfer.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Qur’anic verses, prophetic sayings and prayers are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten by learners.
Keep religious explanations within the wording of the story; do not extend theology or open debates the chapter does not raise.

Preserve the chapter’s source frames: “According to Islamic scholars”, “It is reported that”, “It is said to”, “It was narrated that”, “Although we don’t know the whole story”. A reported detail must not become a plain fact.
Prophets are never portrayed, acted out or drawn by learners; freeze-frames, if used, show ordinary modern situations only.
Discuss the first murder (Chapters 13–15) calmly and factually; never role-play threats or violence and do not dwell on physical details.
Color, origin and ethnicity are discussed only to reject superiority, as Chapters 2 and 5 do; never ask learners to rank groups.
Do not introduce legends, names, places or biographical details that are not in this B2 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Shared Humanity
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Adam (pbuh) raises questions every society faces: Whether any group is better than another by origin, how knowledge creates responsibility, how people repair mistakes and how guidance is passed on to the next generation.

themes.title: One origin, no superiority:
themes.description: Chapter 2 concludes that people “are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors”, and Chapter 5 says Allah “does not focus on origins, that is, race, color, or ethnicity”. Connect this with fair treatment in school, sport and online spaces.

themes.title: Knowledge and responsibility:
themes.description: Chapters 3–4 link knowledge with “science, technology, and culture” and present two kinds of knowledge that “complete one another”. Discuss how knowledge can serve people rather than give status.

themes.title: Stewardship of the Earth:
themes.description: Chapter 11 says Adam “had to maintain, cultivate, construct, and populate the Earth”. Connect this with caring for shared spaces and resources today.

themes.title: Admitting mistakes and repairing harm:
themes.description: Chapter 9 shows regret turning into return and changed direction. Discuss what honest repair looks like between individuals, groups and communities.

actions: Write three class rules that make it clear no one is judged by origin, color or accent, and explain one rule with “because”.
Plan one small stewardship action for the school (a garden bed, a recycling corner, a tidy shared space) and write who has to do what.
Write a short “legacy note” for next year’s class: One useful piece of knowledge and one warning you would pass on.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the argument, is …
One claim I made today that I should qualify (with may, according to, or it is reported that) is …

miniProject.title: Claims, Sources and Limits
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one theme from the book (shared origin, knowledge and responsibility, repentance, self-control or legacy). Make a one-page poster or a two-minute audio report: Quote one sentence from the book with its chapter, explain what it means in plain English, add one clearly marked interpretation (“This suggests …”) and one detail the book does not state. Finish with a realistic school application. Use at least three Language Focus patterns such as “not … but rather …”, “according to …” or “except for …”.

reflectivePrompt.title: Where Should We Find Our Value?
reflectivePrompt.desc: The book ends with the question “Where should man truly find his sense of value?” and argues that value does not come from origin. Write eight to ten sentences: What gives a person value in your view, which chapter evidence supports or challenges your view, and one action that shows this value at school. Qualify at least one claim and include one concession (Although …, …).

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values genuinely supported by the chapter. Require evidence first, then connect the value to an observable, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect / D10 Humility
items.value: Rejecting superiority based on origin and contrasting humility with arrogance (Chapters 2, 4–5, 17).

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Admitting mistakes and keeping source boundaries visible in learners’ own language (Chapters 8–10, 12).

items.label: D12 Patience / D9 Compassion
items.value: Self-control and compassion under pressure, treated as choices with consequences (Chapters 13–15).

items.label: D16 Responsibility / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Knowledge, stewardship and the passing on of guidance as responsibilities (Chapters 3, 11, 16).

practice: Chapter 5 (Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II): Find the sentence that says the prostration is not worship and the reason given.
Chapter 11 (Adam (pbuh)’s Life on Earth): Find the one thing that eased Adam’s grief.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 85 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (50 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.chapter: Chapter 5: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
peerObservation.focus: Explain the prostration as obedience to Allah and respect for Adam (pbuh), not worship.
lookFor: Instruction: In groups of four, make an argument map on A3 paper: claim, reason, counter-evidence and principle. Write a quoted phrase and the joining linker in each box.
Check questions: How many boxes? (four) / What else goes in each box besides the phrase? (the linker)

While learners work: Give roles: reader, writer, checker, presenter. Check that the counter-evidence box uses Adam’s humble origin from the text. Listen in Activity 3 for learners who explain why “Although … yet” is wrong.
Evidence of “Argument accuracy”: Explains why the prostration is respect and obedience, not worship.

peerObservation.chapter: Chapter 12: The Conflict of Habil and Qabil
peerObservation.focus: Explain why Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted, according to the chapter, without linking acceptance to occupation.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, complete the three-layer table: narration, verse and the writer’s comments on the source. Check where the names of the brothers appear and where they do not.
Check questions: How many layers? (three) / What do you check about the names? (where they appear)

While learners work: Check that pairs notice that the verse gives no names. Listen during Activity 1 for learners who say why the doer is hidden. In the Use task, check that the conclusion stays inside the evidence.
Evidence of “Reason for the outcome”: Gives the text’s reason for the outcome: insincerity.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.

Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

actionResearch.question: Can learners report a claim with the right source frame (Chapter 10: X said vs It is said to …) in their own writing?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 10 transfer task, count learners who rewrite the local claim with a correct source frame.

content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the introduction by what they do (name the source, put the topic first with a passive, reject or narrow an idea), rewrite three sentences with rather than and active verbs (tells, portray), then choose the summary that keeps “a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah”. whatToNotice: The chapter moves in steps: Terms, a definition of mud, a verse, a hadith, a conclusion, then a correction.
