Read again and mark the verse, the hadith with its reference, and the writer’s conclusion in three colors.
Open the picture hotspots “Shared Human Origin” and “Human Capacities” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the three terms and what mud is a mixture of.
Paragraph 2: find the colors in the hadith and the conclusion the writer draws from it.
Paragraph 3: find what the writer rejects about Adam’s (pbuh) origin and which abilities he was given.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: composition, mixture, superiority, ancestor, species.
“they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors.” What exactly does the writer rule out here?
Write one sentence with ancestor and one with composition.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about where the information on colors comes from. Compare the verse at the end of paragraph 1 with the saying at the start of paragraph 2.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the verse of Surah Sad again. What does it say Adam (pbuh) was created from?
Read the hadith. Where do the colors appear?
Decide which source the statement names, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain how earth, water and clay are related?
Can I say which source lists colors?
Can I explain why there is a comma before “which is a mixture of water and soil”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in 6–8 sentences a concept that can be described in more than one way. Use a relative clause, one passive, an example marker, and a conclusion with therefore or so that your evidence really supports.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter concludes that color gives no one superiority. What would change in a class or a team if everyone acted on this idea?

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
objectives: I can explain the qualities Adam (pbuh) needed to be a representative.
I can tell a direct interpretation (shows, means) from a careful one (points to, could be).
I can report the writer’s interpretation without making it stronger or weaker.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort sentences by whether the writer states the meaning directly or only suggests it, correct two passive forms (“had to be taught”, “The names taught to …”), then choose the summary that keeps the writer’s level of certainty. The last activity asks you to write a qualified interpretation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: rep-re-SEN-ta-tive, ex-TRAOR-di-nar-y, fun-da-MEN-tal, civ-i-li-ZA-tion, in-TEL-li-gence. Read the angels’ reply slowly and humbly, starting with “Glory be to You!”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Taught All the Names”. What might “all the names” include? Listen once to the verse and notice who speaks each line. Read the last paragraph again and mark shows, means, points to, could be and refer to.
discussionPoints: The angels said they knew only what they had been taught. How does your learning change if you see knowledge as a gift, not only as your own achievement?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Taught All the Names” and “Knowledge and Civilization”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one part at a time: The spirit, the angels’ reply, the word all. The spirit is in paragraph 1, the reply is in the verse, and “all the names” is discussed in paragraph 3. Read the sentence that explains each part, then match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences that begin with evidence, move from a direct meaning (shows, signifies) to an inference (points to), and end with one possibility (could, may) that stays inside the evidence.

whatToNotice: The chapter has three layers: What Allah did, the verse (Baqarah: 31-33), and the writer’s reading of it.
Notice “The names taught to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human”. Could be offers one possible reading, not a certain one.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Taught All the Names”. What might “all the names” include?
Listen once to the verse and notice who speaks each line.
Read the last paragraph again and mark shows, means, points to, could be and refer to.
Open the picture hotspots “Taught All the Names” and “Knowledge and Civilization” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find two things that made Adam (pbuh) special and what breathing the spirit shows.
Paragraph 2: find what the angels admit about their own knowledge.
Paragraph 3: find what the names could be and what knowledge is the basis of.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: representative, extraordinary, fundamental, civilization, intelligence.
“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.” What does this reply show about the angels?
Write one sentence with fundamental and one with intelligence.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match three parts of the account with what the chapter says they show. Each part is in a different paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one part at a time: The spirit, the angels’ reply, the word all.
The spirit is in paragraph 1, the reply is in the verse, and “all the names” is discussed in paragraph 3.
Read the sentence that explains each part, then match again.
selfCheck: Can I name the qualities Adam (pbuh) needed?
Can I rank shows, points to and could be by strength?
Can I explain why the writer says “he had to be taught by Allah”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences that begin with evidence, move from a direct meaning (shows, signifies) to an inference (points to), and end with one possibility (could, may) that stays inside the evidence.
content.reflectionPrompt: The angels said they knew only what they had been taught. How does your learning change if you see knowledge as a gift, not only as your own achievement?

objectives: I can explain the two types of knowledge and the job of each.
I can explain why the writer calls them complementary, not alternatives.
I can use require and necessary for with a to-infinitive accurately.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide whether the writer presents worldly knowledge and revelation as alternatives (he does not), correct two verb patterns (“required even the angels to prostrate”, “necessary for mankind to maintain”), then complete the lines with However, which, through and both. The last activity asks you to write a complementarity argument.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: OFF-spring, rev-e-LA-tion, es-SEN-tial, PRIV-i-lege, AR-ro-gant. Read the dialogue in the verses with a different voice for each speaker, and let “I am better than he” sound proud.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Two Forms of Knowledge”. Which two forms does it mean? Listen once for the two kinds of knowledge and the turn to the story: “the tale reaches its rising action”. Read the verses again and write who speaks each line: Allah, the angels or Satan.
discussionPoints: Satan judged his value by what he was made of. What weak criteria do people use today to feel better than others?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Two Forms of Knowledge” and “Refusing to Bow Down”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the sentence that begins “One is necessary for mankind …”. Read only the half about revelation, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences about two resources or skills with different but complementary jobs. Use however, not … but rather …, both and one necessity expression, and avoid a false either/or.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the knowledge Allah gave Adam (pbuh), to revelation, to the angels’ prostration, then to Satan’s refusal in the verses.
Notice “These two types of knowledge are not alternatives to each other, but rather they complete one another.” The writer rejects an either/or reading.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Two Forms of Knowledge”. Which two forms does it mean?
Listen once for the two kinds of knowledge and the turn to the story: “the tale reaches its rising action”.
Read the verses again and write who speaks each line: Allah, the angels or Satan.
Open the picture hotspots “Two Forms of Knowledge” and “Refusing to Bow Down” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find why Adam (pbuh) and his offspring are considered higher than other beings.
Paragraph 2: find how revelation reaches mankind and what each kind of knowledge is for.
Paragraph 2: find the reason Satan gives for refusing to prostrate.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: offspring, revelation, essential, privilege, arrogant.
“I am better than he (Adam); You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.” What criterion does Satan use to judge value?
Write one sentence with essential and one with privilege.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what revelation helps people understand. Look in paragraph 2 for the sentence that gives each kind of knowledge its own job.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find the sentence that begins “One is necessary for mankind …”.
Read only the half about revelation, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name the job of each kind of knowledge?
Can I explain why either would be the wrong word in “both types of knowledge”?
Can I use “necessary for mankind to maintain” as a pattern in my own sentence?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences about two resources or skills with different but complementary jobs. Use however, not … but rather …, both and one necessity expression, and avoid a false either/or.
content.reflectionPrompt: Satan judged his value by what he was made of. What weak criteria do people use today to feel better than others?

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
objectives: I can explain why the angels’ prostration was not worship.
I can explain how the writer answers Iblis’ claim with evidence.
I can use which is, in other words and that is to make key words precise.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four clarifications with what they explain (which is faith or Islam, in other words, that is, and a sentence that widens a category), rewrite two sentences with Although and therefore, then sort parts of the chapter into reasons (because, since) and contrasting views (On the other hand, yet). The last activity asks you to challenge a weak criterion.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: in-a-BIL-i-ty, o-BE-di-ence, ad-mi-RA-tion, HUM-ble, eth-NIC-i-ty. Read “that is, race, color, or ethnicity” as one group, with a short pause before it.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “False Superiority”. What makes a superiority false? Listen once for the two halves of the chapter. Read again and mark every because, since and yet, and each clarifying phrase (which is, in other words, that is).
discussionPoints: Adam’s (pbuh) humble origin shows that origin does not decide a person’s value. How can you judge people by what they do rather than where they come from?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Knowledge and Obedience” and “False Superiority”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go to the last sentence of paragraph 2. Find the word yet. Read what comes after it, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–8 sentences about a claim that judges people, ideas or achievements by a weak criterion. Define the criterion with that is or in other words, explain it with because, turn with on the other hand, and challenge it with yet.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two halves: The angels’ response (paragraph 1) and Iblis’ arrogance (paragraph 2), joined by “On the other hand”.
Notice “yet Adam (pbuh)’s humble origin shows that Allah does not focus on origins”. After yet, the writer sets evidence against Iblis’ claim.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “False Superiority”. What makes a superiority false?
Listen once for the two halves of the chapter.
Read again and mark every because, since and yet, and each clarifying phrase (which is, in other words, that is).
Open the picture hotspots “Knowledge and Obedience” and “False Superiority” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the angels realized and what Adam’s (pbuh) knowledge included.
Paragraph 1: find why the prostration was not worship and what it meant instead.
Paragraph 2: find where Iblis’ arrogance came from and when it came to the surface.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: inability, obedience, admiration, humble, ethnicity.
“all humans ultimately originate from dried mud.” Why does this fact weaken any claim based on race or color?
Write one sentence with obedience and one with admiration.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what the writer uses to answer Iblis’ claim. Read the last sentence of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go to the last sentence of paragraph 2.
Find the word yet.
Read what comes after it, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the prostration was not worship?
Can I say what “that is” makes concrete in the last sentence?
Can I rewrite the because sentence about the prostration so that it uses therefore?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–8 sentences about a claim that judges people, ideas or achievements by a weak criterion. Define the criterion with that is or in other words, explain it with because, turn with on the other hand, and challenge it with yet.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam’s (pbuh) humble origin shows that origin does not decide a person’s value. How can you judge people by what they do rather than where they come from?

objectives: I can explain the freedom and the single limit given in the Garden.
I can contrast the two paths of Adam (pbuh) and Satan.
I can explain what will expresses in Satan’s words.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match lines from the verses with what they do (tell where to live, give wide freedom, forbid one thing, warn, ask for time), rewrite the narrator’s While sentence with whereas and a full clause (because he challenged), then choose what will expresses in “I will deceive them all” (a firm intention). The last activity asks you to contrast two paths with boundaries and intentions.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: re-SPECT-ful, in-HAB-it, WRONG-do-ers, OUT-cast, GRATE-ful. Read Satan’s four directions evenly: “from before them, and from behind them, and from their right, and from their left”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Satan’s Vow”. What does Satan swear to do? Listen once and note who speaks in each verse. Read paragraphs 3–5 again and mark what is allowed, what is forbidden and what is requested.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) had wide freedom and only one limit. Why can one clear limit protect freedom rather than reduce it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Life in the Garden” and “Satan’s Vow”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read paragraph 4 for the first step. In the last paragraph, write who speaks each line: Allah or Satan. Order the steps again: who asks, who grants, and when the oath comes.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences about two people, groups or choices that move in different directions. Include one boundary, one while contrast, a clear statement that the paths differ, and two will forms that show intention.

whatToNotice: The chapter is built from verses, with short narrator sentences between them: One origin, life in the Garden, one forbidden tree, then Satan’s path.
Notice “While Satan reached the point of no return by challenging his Creator, Adam (pbuh) took a path completely different from him.” This narrator sentence sets two paths side by side.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Satan’s Vow”. What does Satan swear to do?
Listen once and note who speaks in each verse.
Read paragraphs 3–5 again and mark what is allowed, what is forbidden and what is requested.
Open the picture hotspots “Life in the Garden” and “Satan’s Vow” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 3: find the permission, the limit and the warning in A’raf, verse 19.
Paragraph 4: find the four directions from which Satan says he will come.
Paragraph 5: find what Satan asks for and what he is given.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: respectful, inhabit, wrongdoers, outcast, grateful.
“and you will not find most of them grateful to You.” What does Satan predict about people?
Write one sentence with inhabit and one with grateful.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order the steps of Satan’s story. Start with paragraph 4, then follow the conversation in the verses of Surah Sad in the last paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read paragraph 4 for the first step.
In the last paragraph, write who speaks each line: Allah or Satan.
Order the steps again: who asks, who grants, and when the oath comes.
selfCheck: Can I name the one limit inside the freedom?
Can I explain the two paths with while?
Can I explain why will in “I will deceive them all” is a firm intention, not a prediction?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 7–9 sentences about two people, groups or choices that move in different directions. Include one boundary, one while contrast, a clear statement that the paths differ, and two will forms that show intention.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) had wide freedom and only one limit. Why can one clear limit protect freedom rather than reduce it?

objectives: I can explain how the writer links human nature to Adam’s (pbuh) decision.
I can tell a general truth (present simple) from an event in the story (past simple).
I can use a condition, might and the past perfect to show doubt and order.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter into truths about people in general and events in this story, rewrite two sentences (expand trying to persuade into a full clause, and turn As soon as into No sooner … than), then choose eat, might and had warned. The last activity asks you to write a vulnerability, decision and consequence paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: de-ter-mi-NA-tion, im-MOR-tals, sin-CERE, pre-OC-cu-pied. Read Adam’s (pbuh) question with real doubt: “What will happen if I eat from this tree?”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Weakening Determination”. What makes determination weaker? Listen once for the steps from whisper to decision. Read again and mark every present simple verb and every past perfect.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) and Eve were preoccupied with the tree for years. How do repeated small thoughts make a bad choice feel normal?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Weakening Determination” and “The Forbidden Tree”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Find the sentence that begins “On the other hand, Satan would seek …”. Read what comes after because, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person who is slowly persuaded into a poor decision. Start with a general tendency, explain a motive with because, add an if condition and a might possibility, then show the result with the past perfect and as soon as.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from a truth about people in general, to Satan’s motive and method, to Adam’s (pbuh) doubt, to the decision and its result.
Notice “man tends to forget. His heart changes, and his determination weakens.” The present simple inside a past story states a truth about all people.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Weakening Determination”. What makes determination weaker?
Listen once for the steps from whisper to decision.
Read again and mark every present simple verb and every past perfect.
Open the picture hotspots “Weakening Determination” and “The Forbidden Tree” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find why Satan wanted to remove Adam (pbuh) from mercy and how he did it.
Paragraph 2: find Satan’s two false claims and the question Adam (pbuh) asked himself.
Paragraph 2: find what they forgot and what Adam (pbuh) felt as soon as he had eaten.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: determination, whispered, immortals, sincere, preoccupied.
“I am a sincere advisor to you.” Why is it ironic that Satan uses the word sincere?
Write one sentence with preoccupied and one with determination.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Satan wanted to remove Adam (pbuh) from mercy. Look in paragraph 1 for the sentence with because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Find the sentence that begins “On the other hand, Satan would seek …”.
Read what comes after because, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the present simple appears in a past story?
Can I say why Adam (pbuh) uses might, not must?
Can I explain what “had warned” shows about time?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person who is slowly persuaded into a poor decision. Start with a general tendency, explain a motive with because, add an if condition and a might possibility, then show the result with the past perfect and as soon as.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) and Eve were preoccupied with the tree for years. How do repeated small thoughts make a bad choice feel normal?

objectives: I can explain what Adam (pbuh) and Eve did when they realized their mistake, and why.
I can explain what each question and reply in the dialogue does.
I can separate what the Qur’an says from what scholars add.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four lines of the dialogue with what they do (remind of a warning, ask what a reaction means, reject one explanation and give the real one, cry urgently for mercy), complete the narrator’s lines with When, so and because, then sort the last paragraph into what the Qur’an says or does not say and what scholars add. The last activity asks you to write a source-aware explanatory paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: de-CEP-tion, EV-i-dent, un-CLAD, in-BORN, for-BID-den. Read “Forgiveness! Forgiveness!” as an urgent plea, then “No, my Lord, but I am shy of You.” quietly and humbly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Recognition and Modesty”. What is the sense of shame (haya)? Listen once for the chain: discovery, response, reason. Read paragraph 4 again and mark what the Qur’an says, what it does not say, and what scholars say.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) said he was not running away but shy before Allah. What is the difference between hiding from a mistake and feeling ashamed of it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Recognition and Modesty” and “Turning Back to Allah”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the sentence with “in haste”. Read what follows because, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a claim you know from a source. Give one detail it states, one it does not specify, one interpretation with according to, a clarification with that is, and a reminding question answered with No, … but ….

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the verse, to the narrator’s explanation, to a short dialogue, then to a note on sources.
Notice “This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an. It is only mentioned that Satan deceived Adam (pbuh) and Eve.” The writer marks what the source leaves out before he gives the scholars’ view.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Recognition and Modesty”. What is the sense of shame (haya)?
Listen once for the chain: discovery, response, reason.
Read paragraph 4 again and mark what the Qur’an says, what it does not say, and what scholars say.
Open the picture hotspots “Recognition and Modesty” and “Turning Back to Allah” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 2: find what Adam (pbuh) discovered and what they both did at once.
Paragraph 3: find Adam’s (pbuh) cry and his answer to Allah’s question.
Paragraph 4: find when, according to Islamic scholars, the incident happened.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: deception, evident, unclad, inborn, forbidden.
“the sense of shame (haya) is inborn human nature”. What does inborn add to the explanation?
Write one sentence with evident and one with deception.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why they hurried to cover themselves. Read the end of paragraph 2.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find the sentence with “in haste”.
Read what follows because, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the reason for their haste?
Can I say what “Did I not forbid you” does in the dialogue?
Can I show which claim belongs to the scholars, not to the Qur’an?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a claim you know from a source. Give one detail it states, one it does not specify, one interpretation with according to, a clarification with that is, and a reminding question answered with No, … but ….
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) said he was not running away but shy before Allah. What is the difference between hiding from a mistake and feeling ashamed of it?

objectives: I can explain how regret, repentance and forgiveness are linked in the chapter.
I can explain what unless means in the prayer.
I can move from what people are capable of to what they must do.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the meaning of “Unless You forgive us” (if You do not forgive us), rewrite two sentences with because of and an active verb (Allah forgave …), then correct three forms: “had done”, neither … nor, and “must recognize”. The last activity asks you to write about responsibility and recovery after a mistake.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: re-GRET-ted, MER-cy, re-PENT-ance, PROPH-et-hood, HON-oured. Read the prayer slowly, with a pause after “we have done wrong to ourselves”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Forgiveness Granted”. What was the reason for this forgiveness? Listen once for the steps from regret to prophethood. Read paragraph 2 again and mark the time words (At that time, After a period of time, when).
discussionPoints: The chapter says Adam’s (pbuh) regret was itself the reason for Allah’s mercy. What makes an apology real rather than only words?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Forgiveness Granted” and “Prophethood on Earth”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one part at a time. The regret and the words are near the verses; the community comes after the descent; the lesson is in the last sentence. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person or group that makes a mistake and responds responsibly. State the mistake honestly, add a condition and a cause, move from can to must, and end with a concrete change of direction.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 is built around verses; paragraph 2 explains them and ends with a lesson for all people.

Notice “humans are open to sinning and sometimes rebelling against their Lord. However, in order to remain an honored human, they must recognize their mistakes”. The writer moves from what humans can do to what they must do.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Forgiveness Granted”. What was the reason for this forgiveness?
Listen once for the steps from regret to prophethood.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark the time words (At that time, After a period of time, when).
Open the picture hotspots “Forgiveness Granted” and “Prophethood on Earth” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Adam (pbuh) did immediately and what his regret led to.
Paragraph 2: find what the forgiveness means about Allah and Adam (pbuh).
Paragraph 2: find when Adam (pbuh) was given prophethood and the three firsts he became.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: regretted, mercy, repentance, prophethood, honored.
“This unintentional mistake committed by Adam (pbuh) was forgiven by Allah upon his repentance.” Why does the writer call the mistake unintentional?
Write one sentence with repentance and one with honored.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four parts of the chapter with what it says about them. Use the verses in paragraph 1 and the lesson at the end of paragraph 2.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one part at a time.
The regret and the words are near the verses; the community comes after the descent; the lesson is in the last sentence.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the steps from regret to prophethood?
Can I say “Unless You forgive us” with if … not?
Can I explain why one must is followed by three verbs without to?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person or group that makes a mistake and responds responsibly. State the mistake honestly, add a condition and a cause, move from can to must, and end with a concrete change of direction.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says Adam’s (pbuh) regret was itself the reason for Allah’s mercy. What makes an apology real rather than only words?

objectives: I can explain why the writer says the descent was not a humiliation.
I can tell reports with a named source from reports without one.
I can use would for a future seen from the past.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort the reports into those with a named source (Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar) and those with none (It is also reported, It is said to), choose what would shows in the first sentence (a future seen from the past), then correct would violate, was meant to teach and did not imply. The last activity asks you to write about an event with more than one account.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: ibn ab-BAS, ibn U-mar, DIH-na, as-SA-fa, al-MAR-wa. Stress: IN-no-cence, CORN-er-stone, vice-GE-ren-cy, hu-mil-i-A-tion. Read the long brackets in paragraphs 3 and 4 lower and faster than the main sentence.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Places of Descent”. How many places does the chapter mention? Listen once for the writer’s view of the descent. Read paragraphs 2–4 again and mark each report: Who said it, or no name.
discussionPoints: The writer calls the descent an honorable settlement, not a humiliation. How can a hard new start become a place of responsibility?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Responsible Settlement” and “Places of Descent”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find the name in paragraph 2 and the place it goes with. Find the name in paragraph 4 and the places it goes with. Compare them with the statement, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a historical or community event with more than one account. Start from a past viewpoint with would, state a purpose with was meant to, correct one reading with not … but rather …, and attribute two claims in two different ways.

whatToNotice: The chapter first explains the purpose of the experience, then reframes the descent, then lists reports about where it happened.
Notice “It is also reported that Adam (pbuh) descended with the Black Stone”. The impersonal passive passes on a report without naming its source.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Places of Descent”. How many places does the chapter mention?
Listen once for the writer’s view of the descent.
Read paragraphs 2–4 again and mark each report: Who said it, or no name.
Open the picture hotspots “A Responsible Settlement” and “Places of Descent” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the experience was meant to teach Adam (pbuh), Eve and their offspring.
Paragraph 2: find how the writer reframes the descent and what Ibn Abbas said.
Paragraphs 3–4: find the report about the Black Stone and what Ibn Umar said.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: innocence, cornerstone, vicegerency, humiliation, pilgrimage.
“That experience was essential for their life on Earth; it was a cornerstone of their vicegerency.” Why does the writer call a painful experience a cornerstone?
Write one sentence with humiliation and one with cornerstone.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about who reports the descent on As-Safa and Al-Marwa. Compare the report in paragraph 2 with the one in paragraph 4.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find the name in paragraph 2 and the place it goes with.
Find the name in paragraph 4 and the places it goes with.
Compare them with the statement, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the descent was not a humiliation?
Can I tell “Ibn Umar said that” from “It is also reported that”?
Can I explain would in “Allah knew that Adam (pbuh) and Eve would eat”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a historical or community event with more than one account. Start from a past viewpoint with would, state a purpose with was meant to, correct one reading with not … but rather …, and attribute two claims in two different ways.
content.reflectionPrompt: The writer calls the descent an honorable settlement, not a humiliation. How can a hard new start become a place of responsibility?

objectives: I can list Adam’s (pbuh) responsibilities on Earth and say which one comes first.
I can explain the writer’s claim about removing Allah from the human mind.
I can use no sooner … than, above all and means to organize an argument.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the meaning of “No sooner had one ended than another began.” (each struggle was followed at once by a new one), complete the lines with Above all, means and while, then rewrite three sentences with It was necessary for him, does not want … to remember and As soon as. The last activity asks you to write about responsibility in a demanding new environment.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CON-flict (noun), STRUG-gle, GUID-ance, CUL-ti-vate, POP-u-late. In “No sooner had one ended than another began.” stress NO SOONER and ANOTHER.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Struggle on Earth”. Which struggles did Adam (pbuh) face? Listen once and count how many times you hear had to. Read paragraphs 3 and 4 again and mark yet, but and while.
discussionPoints: Adam’s (pbuh) grief was eased by the task of building life on Earth. How can responsibility help a person through a loss?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Struggle on Earth” and “Building Human Life”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Find the words “the removal of Allah from the human mind”. Read to the end of that sentence, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person or group entering a demanding new environment. Use no sooner … than … once, had to twice, rank one duty with above all, contrast two paths with while or yet, and explain one wider consequence with means.

whatToNotice: The chapter builds a list of necessities with had to, ranks one of them with Above all, and ends with the task that eased his grief.
Notice “the removal of Allah from the human mind means the removal of meaning and purpose from human life.” This is the writer’s claim, not a report of an event.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Struggle on Earth”. Which struggles did Adam (pbuh) face?
Listen once and count how many times you hear had to.
Read paragraphs 3 and 4 again and mark yet, but and while.
Open the picture hotspots “Struggle on Earth” and “Building Human Life” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.

Paragraph 2: find the struggles and the practical needs of life on Earth.
Paragraphs 3–5: find the greatest struggle, the two groups in the battle between good and evil, and what eased Adam’s (pbuh) grief.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: conflict, struggle, guidance, cultivate, populate.
“He had to maintain, cultivate, construct, and populate the Earth.” Which of these verbs are about land and which are about people?
Write one sentence with guidance and one with conflict.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what happens when Allah is removed from the human mind. Read paragraph 3.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Find the words “the removal of Allah from the human mind”.
Read to the end of that sentence, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name three things Adam (pbuh) had to do?
Can I explain why Above all is not the same as After all?
Can I rewrite No sooner … than … with As soon as?

content.chapter: Chapter 12: The Conflict of Habil and Qabil
objectives: I can explain why one offering was accepted and the other was not.
I can compare the chapter’s narration with the verse it quotes.
I can show where an account stops and what we do not know.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose why the writer uses the passive in “Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah” (to keep the focus on the sacrifice), rewrite two sentences with on the other hand and without giving their names, then match four phrases with what they signal about the source. The last activity asks you to write a source-aware contrast paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: HA-bil, QA-bil. Stress: WIT-nessed, HAR-mo-ny, SAC-ri-fice, in-sin-CER-i-ty, PI-ous. Read Qabil’s threat with anger, then the reply in the verse calmly: “Allah accepts offerings only from the God-fearing.”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Two Offerings”. What did each son offer? Listen once and follow the path from joy to conflict to threat. Read paragraph 3 again and mark every phrase that limits a claim (without, does not openly mention, according to, Although).
discussionPoints: Qabil could not bear to see his brother happy while he was unhappy. How can jealousy be turned into something better?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Two Offerings” and “From Conflict to Threat”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Read the two sentences about the offerings. Find the reason after because of, and notice when the threat comes. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a dispute, report or historical case. Contrast two positions with while, use one passive for an outcome, give a cause with because of, limit your source with according to or although we do not know, and keep your conclusion inside the evidence.

whatToNotice: The chapter tells the story twice: First in the narrator’s words, then in the verse, which gives no names. The last paragraph explains what the Qur’an leaves out.
Notice “Although we don’t know the whole story”. The writer admits a gap before he states what can be said.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Two Offerings”. What did each son offer?
Listen once and follow the path from joy to conflict to threat.
Read paragraph 3 again and mark every phrase that limits a claim (without, does not openly mention, according to, Although).
Open the picture hotspots “The Two Offerings” and “From Conflict to Threat” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what each son did and why Adam (pbuh) prayed for help.
Paragraph 1: find why Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted and how he reacted.
Paragraph 3: find why the Qur’an does not give the details found in the Torah.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: witnessed, harmony, sacrifice, insincerity.
“Habil offered his best cattle while Qabil offered his worst grain.” What does the contrast between best and worst show about each son?
Write one sentence with harmony and one with insincerity.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Qabil’s offering was not accepted. Look in paragraph 1 for the words because of.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Read the two sentences about the offerings.
Find the reason after because of, and notice when the threat comes. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the offering was not accepted?
Can I explain why the passive here still says “by Allah”?
Can I name one detail the Qur’an leaves out?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a dispute, report or historical case. Contrast two positions with while, use one passive for an outcome, give a cause with because of, limit your source with according to or although we do not know, and keep your conclusion inside the evidence.
content.reflectionPrompt: Qabil could not bear to see his brother happy while he was unhappy. How can jealousy be turned into something better?

content.chapter: Chapter 13: Habil’s Response & Human Moral Capacity
objectives: I can explain how Habil answered a threat without violence.
I can explain the writer’s view of human nature as dual.
I can concede one point and then stress another.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort pairs into the point the writer accepts first and the point he stresses, rewrite two sentences with However and a purpose phrase for Habil’s aim, then correct three forms after It is better that you, if and did not. The last activity asks you to write a measured response to a conflict.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: ag-GRES-sive, po-TEN-tial, MOD-er-ate, dis-o-BE-di-ent, com-PAS-sion. Read Habil’s words to his brother gently, with a pause before “But if you do not”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Good and Evil Within Us”. What does a dual nature mean? Listen once for the verse, the writer’s explanation and Habil’s advice. Read again and mark although, At first glance, However and Thus.
discussionPoints: Habil did not fear his brother, but he did not want him to be hurt either. How can you stand firm in a conflict and still care about the other person?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Habil Rejects Violence” and “Good and Evil Within Us”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go to the end of the chapter. Read from “Habil did not fear his brother’s threats” to the start of his words. Find the phrase that says what Habil hoped for, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a conflict. Begin with a concession (although, even if), describe a possibility with may or might, state the purpose of a response, suggest an alternative, and end with an if clause that makes the consequence clear.

whatToNotice: The chapter starts with the verse, explains it, widens it to all humans, then returns to Habil and his words.

Notice “At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable. However, it is important to remember that humans have the potential for both good and evil.” The writer admits a first impression, then moves to his wider view.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Good and Evil Within Us”. What does a dual nature mean?
Listen once for the verse, the writer’s explanation and Habil’s advice.
Read again and mark although, At first glance, However and Thus.
Open the picture hotspots “Habil Rejects Violence” and “Good and Evil Within Us” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The verse: Find what Habil says he will not do and why.
The middle of the chapter: Find what people can be and where the path to goodness lies.
The end of the chapter: Find the contrast between the brothers and the advice Habil gives.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: pious, aggressive, potential, moderate, disobedient, purity.
“The path to goodness is in controlling evil thoughts and actions and being moderate in desires.” What two things does the writer ask of people?
Write one sentence with potential and one with purity.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Habil spoke to his brother. Read the sentences just before his words at the end of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go to the end of the chapter.
Read from “Habil did not fear his brother’s threats” to the start of his words.
Find the phrase that says what Habil hoped for, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain Habil’s answer to the threat?
Can I explain what “At first glance” and “may seem” do together?
Can I explain why Habil says “if you do not” and not if you will not?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a conflict. Begin with a concession (although, even if), describe a possibility with may or might, state the purpose of a response, suggest an alternative, and end with an if clause that makes the consequence clear.
content.reflectionPrompt: Habil did not fear his brother, but he did not want him to be hurt either. How can you stand firm in a conflict and still care about the other person?

objectives: I can follow the events from the failed request to the ravens.
I can explain how the verb forms show Qabil’s growing burden.
I can use nor with inversion, the passive and reported speech accurately.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter into a state already reached and something still going on, rebuild the first sentence with “nor did he show”, then correct three forms (“were given up”, “had to be preserved”, “he was not”). The last activity asks you to write about consequence and realisation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: fa-MIL-ial, CRIM-i-nal, CORPSE, GUILT, vic-TO-ri-ous. Read “nor did he show fear of Allah’s punishment” with the stress on NOR and DID.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Two Ravens”. Why did Allah send them? Listen once. Paragraph 1 describes a killing; read it calmly. Read paragraphs 4 and 5 again and mark had lessened, was burdened, was getting and started to.
discussionPoints: The ravens showed that human dignity must be preserved even after death. Where do we protect people’s dignity when they cannot protect it themselves?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Crime and Its Weight” and “The Two Ravens”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Paragraph 1: what happens after the request? Paragraph 4: what does Qabil do with the body? Paragraph 5: what happens between the two ravens? Order the events again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about someone who ignores several restraints, faces a growing consequence and learns from an unexpected example. Use not … nor …, one passive, one developing state with was getting, and one purpose with to show.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the crime, to the verse, to Adam’s (pbuh) search, to Qabil’s burden, and ends with the lesson of the ravens.
Notice “His anger had now lessened, and his heart was burdened with guilt.” These forms show a state already reached; the next sentences show a burden that is still growing.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Two Ravens”. Why did Allah send them?
Listen once. Paragraph 1 describes a killing; read it calmly.
Read paragraphs 4 and 5 again and mark had lessened, was burdened, was getting and started to.
Open the picture hotspots “The Crime and Its Weight” and “The Two Ravens” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find two restraints that did not stop Qabil and how he killed his brother.
Paragraph 4: find what Qabil replied to his father and what Adam (pbuh) understood.
Paragraph 5: find why Allah sent the ravens and what the victorious raven did.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: familial, criminal, corpse, guilt, victorious.
“to show that human dignity had to be preserved even after death”. What does this tell us about the purpose of the ravens?
Write one sentence with guilt and one with familial.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put five events in order. Follow Qabil from the start of the chapter to the ravens at the end.
wrongAnswerSupport: Paragraph 1: what happens after the request?
Paragraph 4: what does Qabil do with the body?
Paragraph 5: what happens between the two ravens? Order the events again.
selfCheck: Can I name the two restraints Qabil ignored?
Can I explain the difference between “had now lessened” and “was getting tired”?
Can I explain why “nor did he show” has question word order?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about someone who ignores several restraints, faces a growing consequence and learns from an unexpected example. Use not … nor …, one passive, one developing state with was getting, and one purpose with to show.
content.reflectionPrompt: The ravens showed that human dignity must be preserved even after death. Where do we protect people’s dignity when they cannot protect it themselves?

objectives: I can explain what the raven showed Qabil and how he reacted.
I can find the point where the chapter moves from events to interpretation.
I can expand compact clauses (participles, reduced passives, which-clauses).
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “how he might cover the corpse of his brother” describes (a way Qabil did not yet know), expand three compact clauses (Witnessing this, a person dominated by evil, jealousy, which …), then sort parts of the chapter into what happened and the writer’s interpretation. The last activity asks you to move from an event to an interpretation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: PU-ri-fy, FALSE-hood, CON-se-quence, JEAL-ous-y, RIGHT-eous. Read Qabil’s cry “Woe unto me!” with regret, and slow down at “What is essentially being described here”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Shame and Guilt”. What caused these feelings in Qabil? Listen once and mark the moment the chapter changes from story to meaning. Read paragraph 3 again and underline arises from, provides an example and represents.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) lost both sons, yet he prayed for his son and went back to work. What helps a person keep going after a great loss?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Shame and Guilt” and “Adam’s (pbuh) Continued Responsibility”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read each option and ask: Does it tell what someone did, or what the events mean? Go to the start of paragraph 3. Find the sentence with essentially, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about an event that leads to a wider idea about human behavior. Include a purpose, a how-clause, What is essentially described here is …, a which-clause and a while contrast, and keep fact and interpretation apart.

whatToNotice: Paragraphs 1–2 narrate; paragraph 3 steps back and interprets, then returns to Adam (pbuh).
Notice “What is essentially being described here is the consequence of choosing evil.” This wh-cleft signals that the writer is now interpreting, not narrating.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Shame and Guilt”. What caused these feelings in Qabil?
Listen once and mark the moment the chapter changes from story to meaning.
Read paragraph 3 again and underline arises from, provides an example and represents.
Open the picture hotspots “Shame and Guilt” and “Adam’s (pbuh) Continued Responsibility” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find why Allah sent the raven.
Paragraph 2: find what Qabil said and what was also a first.
Paragraph 3: find what jealousy defeats, what Qabil and Habil represent, and why Adam (pbuh) turned to worldly matters.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: purify, falsehood, consequence, jealousy, righteous.
“choosing the truth over falsehood and goodness over evil will purify human nature of evil.” Which condition does the writer give just before this?
Write one sentence with jealousy and one with consequence.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks which sentence interprets rather than reports. Look at the start of paragraph 3.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read each option and ask: Does it tell what someone did, or what the events mean?
Go to the start of paragraph 3.
Find the sentence with essentially, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I say what the raven showed Qabil?
Can I point to the sentence where interpretation begins?
Can I expand “Witnessing this” into a full time clause?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about an event that leads to a wider idea about human behavior. Include a purpose, a how-clause, What is essentially described here is …, a which-clause and a while contrast, and keep fact and interpretation apart.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) lost both sons, yet he prayed for his son and went back to work. What helps a person keep going after a great loss?

objectives: I can describe Adam’s (pbuh) role as a prophet and father in his last years.
I can tell a narrated detail from a direct claim.
I can move between reported and direct speech with would and will.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide whether “It was narrated that …” presents the detail about Seth as passed on by others (it does), correct three forms (calling, by telling, tempted Qabil to kill), then rewrite Adam’s (pbuh) reported words as direct speech with will not leave and will be united. The last activity asks you to write a careful legacy paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Name: SETH. Stress: suc-CES-sor, SCROLLS, TEMPT-ed, LEG-a-cy, ap-PRO-pri-ate. Read the numbers as one hundred and four and fifty, and read the last sentence slowly and calmly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Adam’s (pbuh) Legacy”. What did he leave his children? Listen once for his three activities as a prophet (advising, telling, calling). Read paragraph 2 again and mark every would.
discussionPoints: Adam’s (pbuh) legacy was the promise that people would not be left alone without guidance. What do you want to pass on to the people who come after you?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Seth Takes Over” and “Adam’s (pbuh) Legacy”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one name at a time. Iblis and Seth are in paragraph 1; the prophets and the Angel of Death are in paragraph 2. Read the sentence with each name, then match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person or institution passing values to a later generation. Use two parallel -ing phrases, one reporting frame, two would forms and different …, but united in …, and keep reports apart from your own view.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 describes his work as a prophet and the choice of a successor; paragraph 2 gives his last message and his death.
Notice “It was narrated that when Adam (pbuh)’s death drew near, he appointed his son Seth to be his successor”. The reporting frame shows that the detail comes through narration.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Adam’s (pbuh) Legacy”. What did he leave his children?
Listen once for his three activities as a prophet (advising, telling, calling).
Read paragraph 2 again and mark every would.
Open the picture hotspots “Seth Takes Over” and “Adam’s (pbuh) Legacy” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Adam (pbuh) warned his children about and how.
Paragraph 1: find what Seth was taught and the numbers in the hadith about the scrolls.
Paragraph 2: find what Adam (pbuh) promised about the prophets and how he died.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: successor, scrolls, tempted, legacy, appropriate.
“The prophets would have different names and miracles, but they would be united in one thing”. What is the one thing?
Write one sentence with legacy and one with successor.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four names with what the chapter says about them. Two are in paragraph 1 and two are in paragraph 2.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one name at a time.
Iblis and Seth are in paragraph 1; the prophets and the Angel of Death are in paragraph 2.
Read the sentence with each name, then match again.
selfCheck: Can I describe Adam’s (pbuh) work as a prophet?
Can I explain what “It was narrated that” does?
Can I turn “would not leave man alone” into direct speech?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about a person or institution passing values to a later generation. Use two parallel -ing phrases, one reporting frame, two would forms and different …, but united in …, and keep reports apart from your own view.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam’s (pbuh) legacy was the promise that people would not be left alone without guidance. What do you want to pass on to the people who come after you?

content.chapter: Chapter 17: The Challenge of Satan & Human Value
objectives: I can explain the limits of Satan’s authority in the verses.
I can tell what the writer concedes from what he stresses.
I can explain the book’s final question about human value.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four lines of the verses with their meaning (a broad claim narrowed by except for), rewrite two sentences as a wh-cleft (What makes Satan look so strong is …) and with By learning, then choose the summary that keeps what the writer concedes and what he stresses. The last activity asks you to build a qualified final argument that ends with an open question.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: mis-LEAD, ac-KNOWL-edg-es, au-THOR-i-ty, REB-el (noun), VAL-ue. Read the final question with a real rising tone: “Where should man truly find his sense of value?”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Satan’s Limited Authority”. Over whom does Satan have no authority? Listen once and follow the broad claim and the two exceptions in the verses. Read paragraph 3 again and mark the bracket with although and the words but rather.
discussionPoints: The book ends by asking where man should truly find his sense of value. What is your answer after reading the whole story?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Satan’s Limited Authority” and “Where True Worth Lies”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go to the end of paragraph 3. Read the part of the sentence after the semicolon. Compare it with the last line of the verses, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about an influence that looks powerful but depends on people’s choices or habits. Narrow a broad claim with except, concede with although, reframe with but rather or in fact, explain the appearance with it is … that makes … look, and end with a real open question.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the verses of Surah Hijr, to what the tale teaches, to the writer’s claim about Satan’s strength, and ends with a question.
Notice “Satan alone is not strong; it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and carefulness that make Satan look so strong.” The it-cleft moves the cause from Satan to human beings.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Satan’s Limited Authority”. Over whom does Satan have no authority?
Listen once and follow the broad claim and the two exceptions in the verses.
Read paragraph 3 again and mark the bracket with although and the words but rather.
Open the picture hotspots “Satan’s Limited Authority” and “Where True Worth Lies” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The verses: Find Satan’s claim and the two exceptions.
Paragraph 3: find what learning Adam’s (pbuh) tale means and what the Qur’an underlines about Satan.
Paragraphs 4–5: find what the events are like and the question each character raises.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: mislead, acknowledges, authority, rebel, value.
“Over My servants you have no authority, except for the sinners who follow you.” Who comes under Satan’s influence?
Write one sentence with authority and one with value.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what makes Satan look so strong. Find the sentence in paragraph 3 that begins “Satan alone is not strong”, and check the verses too.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go to the end of paragraph 3.
Read the part of the sentence after the semicolon.
Compare it with the last line of the verses, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the two exceptions in the verses?
Can I explain what the writer concedes and what he stresses about Satan?
Can I answer the final question in my own words?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 8–10 sentences about an influence that looks powerful but depends on people’s choices or habits. Narrow a broad claim with except, concede with although, reframe with but rather or in fact, explain the appearance with it is … that makes … look, and end with a real open question.
content.reflectionPrompt: The book ends by asking where man should truly find his sense of value. What is your answer after reading the whole story?

metadata.title: Adam B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Judge • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh) on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the story and the argument of the 17 chapters.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Tell verses, hadiths and reports from the writer’s interpretation.
Use qualified language when the evidence is qualified.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text, not with guesses.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 17.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the story and the argument.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the story and the writer’s point, once to follow the exact wording.
points: First listening: What happens, and what does the writer claim about it?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence or verse and read it with the same pauses and stress.

sections.title: 3. Evidence or Interpretation?
sections.text: This book mixes verses and hadiths, reports passed on by narrators, and the writer’s own interpretation. Learn to tell them apart.
points: A verse or hadith has a reference, such as (Baqarah: 34) or (see Abu Dawud, Sunnah 16).
A report names who passed it on (Ibn Abbas said …) or keeps a distance (It is reported that …, It was narrated that …).
An interpretation says what an event means: shows, points to, could be, What is essentially being described here is ….
Keep your own claims as careful as the evidence.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to work out the meaning yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Use the word in a sentence that explains a cause, a contrast or a choice.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Answer the Quick Challenge before reading the feedback. Then do the four Language Focus activities.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): See what a sentence does in the story or the argument.
Activities 2 and 3 (Build or Analyse): choose, correct, rebuild or rewrite forms from the chapter.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say a B2 paragraph about a different situation.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph or one verse at a time.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Mark events, sources and interpretations in three colors.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book asks where real human value lies. Connect each value to one action.
points: Equal dignity: No one is superior because of color or origin (Chapters 2, 5).
Humility: Knowledge is a gift, not a reason for pride (Chapters 3, 4).
Repentance: Admit a mistake and turn back at once (Chapters 8, 9).
Self-control: Answer anger without violence (Chapter 13).
Responsibility: Choices have consequences, and Satan looks strong only through human weakness (Chapters 15, 17).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 17, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
